So, if he had not had ninety-nine ewes, would it have been permissible for him to say to his brother, "Give me your ewe"?

Thus, this matter has no bearing on the case, because he is a wrongdoer even if he did not have ninety-nine. Thus, Sayyiduna Dawud first judged before hearing from the other party, and then he introduced into the basis of the judgment what has no bearing on it, namely his saying ﴿إِلَىٰ نِعَاجِهِ﴾, for perhaps they were envious of him for having ninety-nine.

And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿وَإِنَّ كَثِيراً مِّنَ الْخُلَطَآءِ﴾ ("Indeed, many of the partners"), i.e., the associates (al-khulata', the partners), ﴿لَيَبْغِيۤ بَعْضُهُمْ عَلَىٰ بَعْضٍ إِلاَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ وَعَمِلُواْ الصَّالِحَاتِ﴾ ("transgress against one another, except those who have believed and done righteous deeds"). The meaning: this case is not a singular or isolated one; rather, it is a phenomenon that occurs frequently among partners. Often one partner transgresses against his partner and wrongs him, even though they became partners only out of mutual love, agreement and understanding. But all this does not prevent a human being's inclination to wrong. Such people are like gamblers: you see them outwardly as beloved friends, while each of them is eager to take what is in the other's pocket.

Then the Exalted draws our attention to the fact that this matter is not absolute; rather, there is another kind of partner who does not wrong. Who are they? They are those whom God excepted by His saying: ﴿إِلَّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ﴾, but they are few: ﴿وَقَلِيلٌ مَّا هُمْ﴾ ("and few are they"), i.e., less than few, or very few...

Then the Exalted says, explaining the state of Sayyiduna Dawud after he passed through this case: ﴿وَظَنَّ دَاوُودُ أَنَّمَا فَتَنَّاهُ﴾ ("And Dawud thought that We had only tried him"), meaning: We tested him and afflicted him. Here ﴿ظَنَّ﴾ (thought) means "knew and was certain." It is as if the Exalted were teaching Dawud the science of judgment and its principles, so He tested him with this matter. It became a trial (fitnah) for him in three respects. First: he feared and was terrified while in the presence of his Lord, from creatures like himself who came upon him, and he thought they would kill him. Second: he judged for the first party before hearing from the other. Third: he introduced into his judgment a basis that had no bearing on the matter.

The word ﴿فَتَنَّاهُ﴾ means: We tested him, from their saying: "He tried the gold over the fire" (fatana al-dhahab 'ala al-nar), to purify it from its base elements.

When Sayyiduna Dawud learned of this, he did not refuse; rather, he sought forgiveness from his Lord for all of that: ﴿فَاسْتَغْفَرَ رَبَّهُ وَخَرَّ﴾ ("So he asked his Lord for forgiveness and fell down"), i.e., he fell to the ground in an involuntary fall. The falling here corresponds to prostration (sujud), not bowing (ruku'); this is why the Exalted said: ﴿يَخِرُّونَ لِلأَذْقَانِ سُجَّداً﴾ ("they fall down upon their chins in prostration") [al-Isra': 107]. Thus the word "kharra" (fell down) gives us both meanings: he fell down prostrating, being in the posture of bowing before he prostrated. And the meaning of ﴿وَأَنَابَ﴾ ("and turned in repentance") is that he returned to God in repentance.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 38, verse 25:

His saying: ﴿Indeed, he has wronged you﴾ [Sad: 24] attributes wrongdoing to one party, ﴿by demanding your ewe be added to his ewes﴾ [Sad: 24]. He introduced something into the basis of the judgment that was not part of the basis of the judgment. So, if he had not had ninety-nine ewes, would it have been permissible for him to say to his brother: "Give me your ewe"?

Therefore, this matter has no bearing on the case, because he is a wrongdoer even if he did not have ninety-nine. Thus, our master Dawud first gave judgment before hearing from the other party, and then he introduced into the basis of the judgment something that had no bearing on it, which is his saying: ﴿to his ewes﴾ [Sad: 24]. Perhaps they were resentful of him for having ninety-nine.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, many of the partners⁠ (khulata', i.e., associates in a joint venture) ﴾ [Sad: 24], meaning: the partners, ﴿do wrong one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [Sad: 24]. The meaning: this case is not a singular or isolated one; rather, it is a phenomenon that frequently occurs among partners. A partner often oppresses his partner and wrongs him, even though they formed the partnership only out of mutual love, agreement and understanding. But all of this does not prevent a person's inclination to wrong others. Such people are like gamblers: you see them outwardly as beloved friends, while each of them is eager to take what is in the other's pocket.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, draws our attention to the fact that this matter is not absolute; rather, there is another kind of partner who does not wrong, and who are they? They are those whom Allah excepted by His saying: ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [Sad: 24], but they are few: ﴿and few are they﴾ [Sad: 24], meaning: fewer than the few, or very few indeed.

The Prophet (ﷺ) relates from his Lord, mighty and majestic is He, in the hadith qudsi: meaning, if injustice and betrayal creep into the partnership, Allah, exalted is He, departs from it, so its blessing is erased, and ruin and loss befall it.

Then He, exalted is He, says, explaining the condition of our master Dawud after he passed through this case: ﴿And Dawud thought that We had only tried him﴾ [Sad: 24], meaning: We tested him and afflicted him. Here "thought" (zanna) means "knew and was certain." It is as though the Truth, glory be to Him, was teaching Dawud the knowledge of judgment and its principles, so He tested him with this matter. It became for him a (trap) concerning three things. First: he was frightened and alarmed while in the presence of his Lord, by creatures like himself who approached him, and he thought they would kill him. Second: he gave judgment for the first party before hearing from the other. Third: he introduced into his judgment a basis that had no bearing on the matter.

And the word ﴿tried him﴾ [Sad: 24], meaning: We tested him, comes from the saying: "fatana al-dhahab 'ala al-nar" (he tested the gold over the fire) in order to purify it from its base elements.

When our master Dawud learned of that, he did not refuse; rather, he asked his Lord for forgiveness for all of that: ﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord and fell down prostrating⁠ (kharra, i.e., fell down)...﴾ [Sad: 24], meaning: he fell to the ground in an involuntary fall. The falling here suits prostration, not bowing; therefore He said: ﴿they fall down upon their chins in prostration﴾ [al-Isra': 107]. So the word kharra gave us both meanings: he fell prostrate, being in the state of bowing before he prostrated. And the meaning of ﴿and turned in repentance﴾ [Sad: 24] is that he returned to Allah in repentance.

Then comes the result: ﴿So We forgave him that﴾ [Sad: 25], meaning: what had occurred from him. ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a near station⁠ (zulfa, i.e., nearness)﴾ [Sad: 25], meaning closeness and rank. It suffices that the mountains glorified Allah along with him, and the birds echoed with him, ﴿and a good return⁠ (ma'ab, i.e., a good place of return)﴾ [Sad: 25], meaning a good destination and place of return.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 38, verse 26:

The word ﴿khalifah﴾ [Sad: 26] here may mean either a khalifah of God on earth in a general sense, since the whole of mankind is a khalifah, though he (peace be upon him) is the foremost of the khulafa', or a khalifah of the prophets in carrying their messages to people. As long as he is a deputy, he is an appointee: if he performs the duty well, it remains with him, and if he does not perform it well, it is taken from him.

The affliction of man is that when things respond to him and causes obey him, he thinks he has become original in the cosmos, forgetting that he is a deputy, not an original. Yet if he remained mindful of his khilafah on earth, and that it is possible he may be removed from the khilafah at any time, he would remain courteous with his Lord who appointed him: ﴿Nay, indeed man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-'Alaq: 6-7].

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So judge between the people in truth﴾ [Sad: 26], it means: as long as you are a khalifah of God on earth, you populate it with rulings and establish truth in it. ﴿So judge between the people in truth and do not follow desire﴾ [Sad: 26]. This is a precious advice for everyone who judges between people: the truth is before you as a lamp that guides you, so place it in its right position, whoever he may be, and do not follow your desire, for desire corrupts opinion.

For this reason, some thinkers paused before the saying of God about our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ): ﴿Nor does he speak from desire. It is not but a revelation that is revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 3-4].

They said: since he is a revelation that is revealed, why does God correct him, as in His saying: ﴿God pardon you! Why did you give them permission...﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43].

And His saying: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what God has made lawful for you?﴾ [al-Tahrim: 1].

And His saying: ﴿He frowned and turned away, because the blind man came to him﴾ [‘Abasa: 1-2].

They said: the Truth, glorified is He, does not correct His Messenger; rather He informs that he has no desire that makes him incline when judging. He (ﷺ) approaches the matter without desire, whether the matter is from God or from one delegated to legislate in it.

When God, exalted is He, wanted to define the task of His Messenger (ﷺ), He defined the task of His Book as a miraculous book that carries the foundations of the method, not its branches, and that it is dominant over the earlier books, because God established that the earlier books were altered and distorted, so He did not entrust them to the believers in them, as He said: ﴿by what they were entrusted with of the Book of God...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44].

The meaning of "istuhfizu" (were entrusted): they were asked to preserve it and preserve its method. The preservation of the revealed Book was an obligation, and an obligation is open to being obeyed or disobeyed, and these disobeyed, altered and distorted, as God said: ﴿and they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13], and those who did not forget distorted: ﴿they distort words from their places﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13]. Among them were those who brought speech from themselves and inserted it into the speech of God: ﴿And indeed among them is a party who distort their tongues with the Book that you may think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book, and they say, "It is from God," but it is not from God, and they speak falsehood against God while they know﴾ [Al 'Imran: 78].

So: such people are not entrusted with preserving the Book of God, and this has been confirmed by this experience. For this reason the Truth, glorified is He, did not entrust the preservation of the Qur'an to the believers in it; rather He undertook its preservation Himself, saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr: 9].

And because God gave His Prophet Muhammad this station, He wanted to make it clear. The Truth, glorified is He, shows the station of His Messenger in the completion of religions, saying: ﴿This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. This is not all; rather He gives him another task, which is the safeguarding of these religions through him and through the scholars who succeed him after him. For this reason He, glorified is He, said: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people and the Messenger may be a witness over you...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

The Messenger bears witness that he conveyed to us, and it is incumbent on us to extend the message of the Messenger of God, so that we bear witness that we have conveyed it to people after him. For this reason the Messenger of God (ﷺ) warns us against a group who will come from those who do not believe in his Sunnah, saying: "Stick to the Book of God; whatever we find in it of lawful we make lawful, and whatever we find in it of unlawful we make unlawful."

When you trace the word "ta'ah" (obedience) in the Qur'an, you find that it has come in several forms.

Sometimes He says: ﴿And obey God and obey the Messenger﴾ [al-Taghabun: 12], repeating the command to obey.

Sometimes He says: ﴿And obey God and the Messenger﴾ [Al 'Imran: 132], without repeating the verb of command.

And sometimes He says: ﴿Obey God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 20].

So the repetition of the command to obey, once for God and once for the Messenger of God, occurs when God has a command in the general matter, such as prayer for example, and the Messenger of God has a command in detailing how to pray. If the command of the Messenger coincides with the command of God, the command comes as one without repetition. If the command is specific to the Messenger of God and nothing from God is related to it, He says: "Obey the Messenger."

For this reason you notice the grandeur of the expression in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, obey God and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾ [al-Nisa': 59]. He did not say "and obey those in authority." Why? To draw our attention to the fact that obedience to those in authority is from within obedience to God, and obedience to the Messenger means that they have no obedience specific to themselves, because there is no obedience to a creature in disobedience to the Creator.

And His saying, ﴿So judge between the people in truth﴾ [Sad: 26].

That is: a general judgment for all people, not specific to you. Here we must mention His saying to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth that you may judge between the people by what God has shown you, and do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾ [al-Nisa': 105].

This verse has a story. It was revealed concerning Zayd ibn al-Simin, who was a trustworthy man although he was a Jew, and concerning Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man and Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq. Qatadah had a coat of mail that was stolen by Ibn Ubayriq, and the Jew Ibn al-Simin was accused of it. After investigating the matter, they found the coat of mail with Ibn Ubayriq, the Muslim, and the innocence of the Jew became clear.

Here people hastened to the Messenger of God so that he would not rule against the Muslim, lest it become a disgrace to the Muslims before the Jews. The Messenger of God hesitated in the matter, so God revealed to him: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth that you may judge between the people﴾ [al-Nisa': 105], meaning all people: Jews, Christians and Muslims. Indeed the Messenger of God ruled against the Muslim and cleared the Jew, and neither the Messenger of God nor the Muslims cared that the Jew would triumph over the Muslim, because the truth is more honourable than this or that.

When the Jews saw the Messenger of God ruling in favour of the Jew and condemning the Muslim, they turned towards Islam, and many of them embraced Islam, foremost among them (Mukhayriq), who declared his Islam and gave all his wealth to the Messenger of God. Then he went out to fight when the call to arms hastened him, before he had prayed to God a single rak'ah. (Mukhayriq) was killed as a martyr in this battle, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said about him: this is the meaning of ﴿So judge between the people in truth...﴾ [Sad: 26].

The meaning of ﴿khalifah...﴾ [Sad: 26] is that God has made us all deputies on earth, and has made for the deputies a khalifah who manages their affairs and judges between them in what they differ about, by the method of the One who appointed all. Or a khalifah for the messengers who preceded him, who alerts to what has been effaced of the processions of truth among creation. Judgment between people is only needed because of disagreement among them; for if they did not disagree they would not seek judgment, and what people do not differ about does not concern the judge, unless they have differed from the supreme Truth, in which case intervention is necessary.

The word ﴿bil-haqq...﴾ [Sad: 26], "truth," means the established thing that does not change. This belongs to God, exalted is He. As for man, his affairs change and do not settle in one state, and we are subject to change. But the ruling that governs human movement, as long as it is from God, is established and does not change. And since God, exalted is He, has completed the favour, perfected the religion and approved Islam, no one may add a correction to it in anything, because such correction is a slander against God's thoroughness in the wisdom of the ruling.

Truth is opposed by falsehood, and falsehood may rise at times, but truth remains the truth until it prevails in the end. God, exalted is He, leaves falsehood to rise at times for a wisdom: that falsehood bites people and burns them with its fire so that the sweetness of truth may appear to them. When the bitterness of falsehood stings them, they turn themselves to seeking the truth.

So: if falsehood rises, truth is higher. God, exalted is He, has struck us a parable that clarifies this matter, saying: ﴿He sends down water from the sky, and the valleys flow according to their measure, and the torrent carries a swelling foam. And from that which they heat in the fire seeking ornament or utensils is a foam like it. Thus God strikes the parable of truth and falsehood. As for the foam, it passes away as scum, but that which benefits people remains upon the earth. Thus God presents the parables﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17].

So: truth is established, and with this stability we understand that the divine methods did not come to make the word of God supreme; rather they came to make the word of those who disbelieved the lowest, and this meaning is clear in His saying: ﴿And He made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest, and the word of God is the highest...﴾ [al-Tawbah: 40]. He did not join the second to the first, and did not say: "and the word of God is the highest." Because the word of God is not something made, but is a established thing, and it is truth from eternity.

Then He, glorified is He, addresses our master Dawud: ﴿And do not follow desire, for it will lead you astray from the way of God...﴾ [Sad: 26]. Desire is the inclination of the self towards something you crave, regardless of any method that governs it. Desire differs among people: even intimate friends who are inseparable in food, drink and inclinations, when they go to buy something, buy different things and varied colours.

Yes, there is a bond that unites them, which is friendship, but their desires differ. If my desire opposes yours, we must return to something on which we do not differ. If that thing on which we do not differ is above us, there is no shame in it. Shame comes when you submit to one who is your equal and make him your judge, and end up with his opinion.

For this reason the Truth, glorified is He, settles this matter by His saying: ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted...﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 71].

We understand that the difference of desires corrupts life on earth, but how does it corrupt the heavens? And why did He begin with the corruption of the heavens before the earth?

They said: yes, because the corruption will extend beyond the corruption of the earth and corrupt the heavens too, meaning that it will corrupt the judgment of God sent down from heaven. Since it will corrupt the judgment of God sent down from heaven, which is the truth, and this corruption precedes the corruption of what is on earth.

For this reason they did not say: ﴿or You make the sky fall upon us in pieces, as you claim﴾ [al-Isra': 92]. That is desire. Had God answered them in what they asked, the heavens and the earth would indeed have been corrupted. It is from God's mercy to creation that He protects their desires within the theoretical methods that govern people in what they differ about, while what is not differed about He left to you to dwell in as you wish.

If you say: why did He leave them the matters on which there is no disagreement? We say: because in them they will arrive at one agreed truth. This is what we see, for example, in the experimental material sciences: they are an open field for all. The Russians are like the Americans, and indeed we see them placing iron barriers around these sciences so that they do not reach others, while some sneak in and steal what others have reached.

So: the matter on which we will agree is not intervened in by the heavens. This matter was judged by our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who gave us an example in himself (ﷺ) in the matter of pollinating palm trees. When he suggested to them not to pollinate the palms, that year they were spoiled and bore no fruit, and he (ﷺ) said: "You are the more knowledgeable of your worldly affairs." Because you will arrive through experiment at one thing, on which you agree and which you steal from others. But in desires, they differ from one person to another, and clash arises from them, cold or hot.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, explains the reason for the prohibition of following desire, saying: ﴿so that it leads you astray from the way of God...﴾ [Sad: 26]. That is: do not follow desire, because following desire leads you astray from the way of God. The Prophet (ﷺ) made this matter clear to us when he drew for the Companions a straight line and drew around it several lines, then recited: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it. And do not follow [other] paths, lest they separate you from His way...﴾ [al-An'am: 153].

Separation of paths arises from disagreement, however slight it may be. (A millimetre) separates the paths: if you draw two lines from one centre and one of them deviates from the other by one millimetre, their separation would result gradually the further they go from the centre. Have you seen, for example, the switchman who changes the course of the train, what does he do? He moves the end of a rail whose thickness does not exceed five millimetres, and this movement results in the train's course being changed from Alexandria to Aswan.

Thus paths separate, and from slight disagreement a great disagreement arises. A small, simple divergence at the centre results in a wide divergence as the distance lengthens. Just as separation occurs among many paths, separation likewise occurs on a single road when it is wide enough to permit separating.

For example, the desert road to Alexandria is a wide road in two directions, and you can travel in one of them in a winding manner, inclining sometimes to the right and sometimes to the left, so that the length of the road increases. For this reason they said: "sawa' al-sabil" (the even path) means that you make both sides equal.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, explains the consequence of straying and deviating from the straight course, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who stray from the way of God will have a severe punishment for having forgotten the Day of Account﴾ [Sad: 26].

So: heedlessness of this Day and forgetting the consequence is the cause of falling into severe punishment. If a person remembered the recompense for an evil deed he would not do it, and if he remembered the reward of a good deed he would not neglect it, nor be lazy in performing it.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 38, verse 27:

It means: We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in vain, but We created them with truth. Therefore you find them firm and unchanging, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿The sun is not to overtake the moon, nor does the night outpace the day; each is in an orbit, swimming along.﴾ [Yasin: 40] Had this creation been otherwise, there would have been collision in every minute and every moment between these celestial bodies and orbits.

As for "the supposition of those who disbelieved" (ẓann alladhīna kafarū), it means that they suppose that they were created in vain. That is their supposition, and it is mere supposition. Had creation been as they suppose, it would not have been creation, because creation must have a purpose in the mind of the Creator before He creates, just as we said that the one who invented the washing machine or the refrigerator, before creating it, determined its function for it, rather than merely creating it. And He said: ﴿Look into what this instrument is fit for.﴾

So the one who made the thing is the one who determines its purpose, and it is He who sets the maintenance rules for his creation. Therefore we say: the misguidance of the whole world arises from their wanting to legislate for themselves the purpose of what God made, and wanting to set for God's creation its maintenance rules, and to ignore what God has laid down, instead of referring the matter to its owner, as you do in worldly affairs, for every maker knows best what keeps his making in good order.

Then comes this threat: ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve, from the Fire.﴾ God, glorified is He, often threatens His creation with the Fire and promises them punishment. Some see in this a kind of harshness, but the truth is that it is a form of mercy and not harshness. It is part of God's mercy towards us that He magnifies the sin, makes the punishment manifest, and places the recompense before the sin occurs, because when you call the recompense to mind, you refrain and do not act. So: the threat and warning are for a wisdom.

After the Mighty and Majestic (al-Haqq, subhanahu) had mentioned the recompense of the disbelievers in the Fire, He willed to mention the opposite, for things are distinguished by their contraries. He willed to set before us this comparison between the disbelievers and the believers who stood firm upon the path of truth, walked upon the Straight Way, from whose hands and tongues people were safe, and who spread security and spread love. How, then, shall we equate them with the corrupt disbelievers?

In this there is an indication from the Truth, subhanahu, as if He were saying to us: Beware lest you equate these with those; beware lest mercy move you toward the corrupt wrongdoers, for if you show compassion to them you have equated them with the believers.

Therefore, we used to respond to the Communists and say to them: Yes, you have avenged yourselves upon your enemies, the capitalists and the feudal lords, and you have done to them terrible deeds. But what of those who died before you could reach them and take revenge upon them? Without doubt they committed injustice and then departed without being punished.

So: it was necessary that you acknowledge a Day on which retribution is exacted from those who were not requited in this world, otherwise you would equate the good-doer with the evil-doer.

And He said: ﴿like the corrupters in the earth..﴾ [Sad: 28] Because Allah, the Exalted, created the earth in the form of righteousness; so if you do not add to it a righteousness that brings ease and happiness to people, then at the very least you should leave it as it is and not corrupt it. The aspects of reform in the cosmos are many, and we gave an example of this with a well of water: either you leave it in a state from which people benefit as it is, or you increase its goodness, such as by building a wall around it to protect it, or by placing upon it a device for raising the water... etc.

As for throwing filth into it, that is corruption.

We also said: If you enter an untouched garden (unuf), meaning one that no one has entered before you, you will find it in its natural state: you will not see a broken tree, nor smell a foul odour in it, even though there are insects, animals and refuse in it... etc. But if a human being enters it, disorder and corruption appear in it. Why?

Because he does not remain upon the righteousness upon which Allah created nature; for he entered it without the method of Allah, and had he entered by the method of Allah, affairs would have been set right.

Then the Truth, subhanahu, emphasises this meaning, saying: ﴿Or shall We make those who are mindful of God like the wicked?﴾ [Sad: 28] The fajir is the dissolute person who deviates from the law that protects him and protects society, just as the date slips out of its skin (fasaqat al-rutbah min qishratihā). The Truth, subhanahu, before protecting society from the dissolute person, protected the dissolute person from society, for the dissolute person is one, while society is many.

So: the individual is the one who benefits from the method of the Truth, and he is the winner.

Also, when a matter touches a person's own self, he turns to the Truth out of necessity, for he will find protection only in the Truth. We once gave an example to university students, saying: Suppose three young men in the stage of adolescence, two of whom went, as we say, "unbridled" (ʿala ḥall shaʿrihim), while the third stood firm upon the method, to the extent that the two were mocking him and saying about him: "This fellow is a [ṣallā] ... [jardal] ... [qafal]..." etc., such words as we hear.

It happened that one of them had a sister. By God, to whom would he give her in marriage? To his licentious friend, or to his committed, upright friend? Without doubt he would prefer the second, because he trusts him and feels secure with him. So: truth must remain truth, and virtue must remain virtue, and the pious and the wicked cannot be equal.

Then the Truth, subhanahu, addresses His Prophet ﷺ to console him, for the stories of the Qur'an came as consolation for him (ﷺ) and as strengthening of his heart:

﴿A Book We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may ponder its verses...﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 38, verse 29:

"The Book" is the Qur'an, and "blessed" (mubarak) is the thing that gives benefit and good beyond what one can imagine from it. You say: "We take from this thing and it does not diminish; we call it blessed (mabruk)..."

The Qur'an is blessed, and its verses are blessed in terms of their outward rulings, because it trains the soul toward uprightness (istiqamah). If you look at this uprightness economically, you will find that it does not cost you anything. Yes, uprightness does not cost you; it is deviation that costs... Then, the Qur'an is blessed from another side: when you interact with its method, and when you love it, the Real (al-Haqq), glorified is He, reveals to you kinds of secrets at which others marvel, and He opens for you wondrous openings. Did Musa (peace be upon him), while being a Prophet of Allah, not marvel at the deeds of the righteous servant (al-'abd al-salih)? The righteous servant was a servant of Allah upon the method of Musa, yet Allah commanded Musa to follow the righteous servant and to learn from him. But he followed him with sincerity and with love, so when Musa followed him with love and sincerity, he learned from him wonders...

As for the meaning of "liyadabbaru ayatih" (that they may ponder its verses): tadabbur (reflection) is that we do not look at the means superficially; rather we look with contemplation, close attention, and consideration of the outcome. We look at the underlying implications and necessary consequences, so that we may derive from the thing the lessons (ibar) it contains... As for His saying: "wa liyatadhakkara ulu al-albab" (and that those of understanding may take heed): i.e., the people of aware minds. Consider here that the Real, glorified is He, alerts the minds and stirs understanding to contemplate His signs in the cosmos. The person across from you, or the one with whom you have a deal, does not alert you to it unless he is confident that you will embrace it; otherwise he would hide it and deceive you. Like one who sells you a good commodity: you see him explaining its merits to you, inviting you to test it and to verify its quality, and alerting your mind to what was hidden from you of it...

So the Real, glorified and exalted is He, calls us to contemplate His signs, reflect upon them, and investigate them, because He, glorified is He, is confident that when we look, when we investigate and when we reflect, we will be convinced by them, and through them we will reach the truth and the correct position. Yet we see some who, faced with certain religious matters, say: "This is a matter beyond inquiry, and reason has no role in it." We say: but we have been commanded to reflect, to contemplate and to consider the cosmos, so there is no harm in our investigating.

Among the remarkable features of the Qur'anic context in mentioning Dawud and Sulayman is that the two share a single matter. If you look at the first verse that mentions our master Dawud, you find it in Surat al-Baqarah in His words: ﴿So they defeated them by Allah's permission, and Dawud killed Jalut...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 251].

And his last mention here, in Surat (Sad): ﴿And We bestowed upon Dawud Sulayman...﴾ [Sad: 30].

Likewise, the first mention of our master Sulayman occurs in Surat al-Baqarah in His words: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Sulayman...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102].

And his last mention in Surat (Sad) in His words: ﴿And We did test Sulayman and placed upon his throne a body; then he turned back [in repentance]﴾ [Sad: 34].

As for His words: ﴿And We bestowed upon Dawud Sulayman...﴾ [Sad: 30]. Al-wahb (الوهْب) is a gift given without return. If you say: "But the whole matter of childbearing is given without return," yes, but the Creator, glorified is He, gives you your essence, and then adds to it another gift, which is the attributes that are available to that essence, such as kingship, wisdom, and others. Therefore, those who seek things other than through their proper causes seek them by way of gift, as in His words: ﴿Grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me...﴾ [Sad: 35].

And His words: ﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir, who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub, and make him, my Lord, pleasing [to You]﴾ [Maryam: 5-6].

When our master Zakariyya asked Allah for a child, he was an elderly man and his wife was barren. All the causes were unfavorable and not suitable for childbearing, so he asked for it as a gift from Allah, not through law and causes. And although causes in themselves are a gift, they are a general gift; but what attaches to the essence of special attributes is considered a special gift.

As for His words: ﴿An excellent servant...﴾ [Sad: 30]. We know that ni'm (نِعْم) is used for praise, and the praise here is by a doctrinal attribute, which is servanthood to Allah, exalted is He. We have previously said that the word "abd" (servant) and "ubudiyyah" (servitude) is a hated word among people, and they have the right to hate it, because servitude to humans is one in which the master takes the best of his servant. But servitude to Allah, exalted is He, is one in which the servant takes from the best of his Master. This is true servitude, which is considered honor and elevation for the servant.

Therefore, when Allah, exalted is He, manifested Himself to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) with the blessing of the Night Journey and the Ascension, He said: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night...﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. It is as if his servitude to his Lord was what brought him to this station.

Therefore, and to Allah belongs the highest comparison, the man who is a master craftsman (ustadh, أسطى) or teacher with apprentices under him draws close to the sincere one who performs his craft well and excels in submission, obedience, and service to him. He therefore singles him out with his skills, does not withhold from him the hidden secrets and subtleties of the craft, and gives him privileges he does not give to others.

Although he, peace be upon him, was a king, his Lord praised him with the attribute of servitude: ﴿An excellent servant...﴾ [Sad: 30]. Then He explained to us the basis of the praise for servitude, saying: ﴿Indeed, he was one who turns back [to Allah] often﴾ [Sad: 30]. That is, one who returns to Allah: if his soul slips into a lapse, he rebukes himself for it, returns to his Lord, and repents to Him. Therefore He, exalted is He, says in explaining repentance: ﴿Repentance from Allah is only for those who do wrong out of ignorance and then repent soon after...﴾ [al-Nisa': 17].

The meaning of "out of ignorance" (بِجَهَالَةٍ) [al-Nisa': 17] is that he did not plan it and did not arrange for the sin. When it happens from him, he does not rejoice in it or openly display it; rather, he grieves and blames himself. ﴿Those are the ones to whom Allah will turn in forgiveness, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise. And repentance is not [accepted] from those who continue to do evil until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor from those who die while they are disbelievers. For those, We have prepared a painful punishment﴾ [al-Nisa': 17-18].

We have given an example of these two types with students of knowledge who used to travel on scholarly missions to France. Among them was one who was upright and committed to Allah's way, but one night a deviant girl surprises him and offers herself to him, continuing to entice him until he commits the sin with her. This is her act, done out of ignorance and without intent or planning. This is unlike the other, who seeks out sin and tracks down the addresses of its practitioners. This is the one who intends the disobedience and strives toward it.

The word "awwab" (أَوَّابٌ) [Sad: 30] means one who frequently returns and turns back. It is an intensive form meaning one who constantly returns to the truth. He did not rejoice in the sin; rather, he regretted it, corrected his error, and set his path right. This is evidenced by His words after it: ﴿When there were displayed before him, at evening, the poised, swift steeds﴾ [Sad: 31].

Al-'ashiyy (العشيّ) is the period from after midday until sunset. What was displayed before him was like a military review in which a commander inspects his troops and forces. The meaning of ﴿al-safinat...﴾ [Sad: 31] is the plural of safin (صَافِن), which is a purebred, noble steed. You can observe the noble steed by its stance: it does not stand on four legs but on three, with grace, as if it is ready to go.

The meaning of ﴿al-jiyad﴾ [Sad: 31] is the plural of jawad (جَوَاد), which is one that is strong and swift. When the poised, swift steeds from his horses and forces were displayed before Sulayman, he said: ﴿Indeed, I have loved the love of good [i.e., horses] over the remembrance of my Lord until they were hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad: 32]. They said: "The good (الخير) here refers to horses, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: [...] And said: [...]" Therefore, when our Lord commanded us to prepare against the enemies of the religion and its way, He said: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you are able of power...﴾ [al-Anfal: 60], meaning general power. Then He singled out horses, saying: ﴿and of steeds of war, by which you may terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy...﴾ [al-Anfal: 60].

So when the horses were displayed before Sulayman, he said: ﴿Indeed, I have loved the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord...﴾ [Sad: 32]. That is, a love not for vanity or pride, like those who raise horses for show, to enter races and gain fame. Rather, I loved them out of remembrance of my Lord and remembrance of my Lord's way, which commanded the preparation of horses, the garrisoning, and the strength that can impose Allah's way on the earth.

As for His words: ﴿And We bestowed upon Dawud Sulayman...﴾ [Sad: 30]. Al-wahb (الوهْب) is a gift given without return. If you say: "But the whole matter of childbearing is given without return," yes, but the Creator, glorified is He, gives you your essence, and then adds to it another gift, which is the attributes that are available to that essence, such as kingship, wisdom, and others. Therefore, those who seek things other than through their proper causes seek them by way of gift, as in His words: ﴿Grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me...﴾ [Sad: 35].

And His words: ﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir, who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub, and make him, my Lord, pleasing [to You]﴾ [Maryam: 5-6].

When our master Zakariyya asked Allah for a child, he was an elderly man and his wife was barren. All the causes were unfavorable and not suitable for childbearing, so he asked for it as a gift from Allah, not through law and causes. And although causes in themselves are a gift, they are a general gift; but what attaches to the essence of special attributes is considered a special gift.

As for His words: ﴿An excellent servant...﴾ [Sad: 30]. We know that ni'm (نِعْم) is used for praise, and the praise here is by a doctrinal attribute, which is servanthood to Allah, exalted is He. We have previously said that the word "abd" (servant) and "ubudiyyah" (servitude) is a hated word among people, and they have the right to hate it, because servitude to humans is one in which the master takes the best of his servant. But servitude to Allah, exalted is He, is one in which the servant takes from the best of his Master. This is true servitude, which is considered honor and elevation for the servant.

Therefore, when Allah, exalted is He, manifested Himself to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) with the blessing of the Night Journey and the Ascension, He said: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night...﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. It is as if his servitude to his Lord was what brought him to this station.

Therefore, and to Allah belongs the highest comparison, the man who is a master craftsman (ustadh, أسطى) or teacher with apprentices under him draws close to the sincere one who performs his craft well and excels in submission, obedience, and service to him. He therefore singles him out with his skills, does not withhold from him the hidden secrets and subtleties of the craft, and gives him privileges he does not give to others.

Although he, peace be upon him, was a king, his Lord praised him with the attribute of servitude: ﴿An excellent servant...﴾ [Sad: 30]. Then He explained to us the basis of the praise for servitude, saying: ﴿Indeed, he was one who turns back [to Allah] often﴾ [Sad: 30]. That is, one who returns to Allah: if his soul slips into a lapse, he rebukes himself for it, returns to his Lord, and repents to Him. Therefore He, exalted is He, says in explaining repentance: ﴿Repentance from Allah is only for those who do wrong out of ignorance and then repent soon after...﴾ [al-Nisa': 17].

The meaning of "out of ignorance" (بِجَهَالَةٍ) [al-Nisa': 17] is that he did not plan it and did not arrange for the sin. When it happens from him, he does not rejoice in it or openly display it; rather, he grieves and blames himself. ﴿Those are the ones to whom Allah will turn in forgiveness, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise. And repentance is not [accepted] from those who continue to do evil until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor from those who die while they are disbelievers. For those, We have prepared a painful punishment﴾ [al-Nisa': 17-18].

We have given an example of these two types with students of knowledge who used to travel on scholarly missions to France. Among them was one who was upright and committed to Allah's way, but one night a deviant girl surprises him and offers herself to him, continuing to entice him until he commits the sin with her. This is her act, done out of ignorance and without intent or planning. This is unlike the other, who seeks out sin and tracks down the addresses of its practitioners. This is the one who intends the disobedience and strives toward it.

The word "awwab" (أَوَّابٌ) [Sad: 30] means one who frequently returns and turns back. It is an intensive form meaning one who constantly returns to the truth. He did not rejoice in the sin; rather, he regretted it, corrected his error, and set his path right. This is evidenced by His words after it: ﴿When there were displayed before him, at evening, the poised, swift steeds﴾ [Sad: 31].

Al-'ashiyy (العشيّ) is the period from after midday until sunset. What was displayed before him was like a military review in which a commander inspects his troops and forces. The meaning of ﴿al-safinat...﴾ [Sad: 31] is the plural of safin (صَافِن), which is a purebred, noble steed. You can observe the noble steed by its stance: it does not stand on four legs but on three, with grace, as if it is ready to go.

Fitna means testing, and fitna in itself is not disliked; what is disliked is that you fail in it and falter in going through it. So what harm is there if We test you and you succeed in the test? The root of fitna is from the testing of gold to purify it. Gold may be mixed with other materials, and we want pure, refined gold. What do we do? We melt the gold in fire so that the dross comes out of it until it becomes pure and clean. Likewise, fitna acts upon people: it refines them so that the good is distinguished from the bad. God tested Solomon just as He tested his father David, peace be upon them both, in the matter of the prayer niche (mihrab).

As for the meaning of: ﴿And We cast upon his throne a body...﴾ [Sad: 34]. The kursi is the throne on which the king sits, and the jasad is the form of a living being. This form is called (jasad) when it is devoid of spirit. The exegetes have several opinions regarding this verse:

They said: Our master David had another son besides Solomon, but he was a corrupt son, like the son of Noah. This son schemed and carried out a coup against Solomon until he took the kingship from him and remained a king for a long period. When God, glorified is He, wished to restore Solomon to his kingship, He cast this corrupt son onto the throne of his seat as a motionless body with no movement in it. That is: after he had been an obeyed and dominant king, he came to have no control even over himself and his limbs. After that, his subjects rebelled against him and killed him, and Solomon came after him.

They also said: Our master Solomon had many concubines. He said: "Tonight I will go round seventy women, and each one will bear me a son who is a horseman riding his horse in the way of God." That is: the whole matter was in goodness and in God, but he did not put the will (of God) first and did not say: "If God wills." So none of them bore a child except one girl, who bore him a body with no movement and no action. This is because the believer is obliged to put God's will first when he resolves upon something in the future, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow, * Except [when adding], "If Allah wills."﴾ [al-Kahf: 23-24].

For when you say, "I will do such and such tomorrow," you have passed judgment on an act of which you own not a single element. You do not guarantee that you will remain alive until you act, nor do you guarantee that circumstances and causes will not change. So when you attach your act to the will of God, you preserve your dignity and clear yourself of falsehood: you have willed, but God did not will.

It seems that kingship tempted Solomon, and some conceit entered him, because he controlled the worlds of humans, jinn, birds and animals, and the whole universe around him obeyed him. Therefore he did not say, "If God wills," and God requited him for that.

Others said: Solomon, peace be upon him, had begotten a son, and the jinn wished him harm, because they feared that he would do to them what Solomon did. So they wanted to kill him, and Solomon did nothing but raise him above the clouds, where he would nurse from the rain. It is as if he, peace be upon him, wished to flee from the decree of God.

They also said: The body is Solomon himself, because an ordinary person has been made by God able to control his own limbs when God wills it: he stands up merely by wanting to stand, and moves merely by wanting to move, without himself knowing what is happening in his organs and joints. So God, exalted is He, gives man an example in himself, to bring closer to him the matters concerning the Truth within the frame of ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11].

So if you, O created being, do what you will, and your limbs respond to you and obey you merely by the intention, without your commanding them to anything, do you find it far-fetched in the case of the Creator, glorified is He, when He says: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82].

Indeed, the Truth, glorified is He, says to a thing: "Be." As for you, you do not say "Be," for God has spared you that, and made the limbs obey you without an order from you, for if you commanded them they would not respond to you; they respond to the Creator, glorified is He. So if the Creator, glorified is He, wishes to strip you of this power, you want to move your hand and cannot; to alert you that it is a gift given to you, not something inherent in you.

God, glorified is He, granted our master Solomon the ability to control his own limbs, then extended this power to control others of his own kind and of other kinds, and gave him control over the whole universe, which responded to him and answered him. That is: the matter was an exaltation in domination over the soldiers of God.

It seems that something entered the soul of Solomon, peace be upon him, so God, glorified is He, wished to draw his attention to the fact that this power is not inherent in you, but is granted to you; I take it away whenever I will, so you cannot control your limbs nor control others. And God cast him for a period as a body on his throne, unable to do anything and commanding nothing.

Since this blessing is a gift from God, who has given you a kingdom that is not fitting for anyone after you, you must remain holding fast to His rope, always turning to the One who gave you this kingdom.

Therefore, it is related that he, peace be upon him, once rode the carpet, and the wind carried him as he willed. Suddenly the carpet tilted with him and nearly threw him off, so he commanded it to level out with him. The carpet said to him: "We have been commanded to obey you only so long as you obey God."

In sum: We tested him because We granted him a kingdom not fitting for anyone after him, but We do not want him to transgress or exalt himself, and the Truth, glorified is He, does not break His word, and He has said, glorified is He: ﴿Nay, indeed, man transgresses * Whenever he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-Alaq: 6-7].

Solomon, peace be upon him, is a human being, so God, glorified is He, wished to establish for us that man holds dominion over his limbs, dominion over those around him, and dominion over a kind other than his own; but all of this is not inherent in him, rather it is granted to him. The proof: God stripped him of this kingdom at a certain moment, and cast him on his throne as a body with no command, no prohibition, and no authority over anything.

When Solomon understood the matter, he returned and turned back: ﴿then he repented﴾ [Sad: 24]. That is: he returned to what he had been before the trial he had passed through.

That is: he returned to the body that has a spirit in it; or he repented and turned back to God and recognized the cause. The meaning admits of both senses: he repented regarding the cause, or he repented regarding the effect. Jasad is the mass and the outward frame in which there is no spirit, and of which God said: ﴿So when I have proportioned him...﴾ [al-Hijr: 29], meaning the body. And from it is His saying, in the story of the Samiri: ﴿So he brought forth for them a calf, a body that lowed...﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88], meaning the form of the calf and its outward appearance, but without a spirit.

If you say: Does such a thing happen to the messengers? That is: does a prophet err and is he corrected? Yes. The shame would be for an equal to correct you; it is no shame for the one above you to correct you. What is wrong with it if the one who corrects Solomon is his Lord, glorified is He, and not you? So it is an honour that God corrects Solomon. Therefore, when the Truth, glorified is He, corrected the ruling for His prophet Muhammad, He said: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what God has made lawful for you, seeking the pleasure of your wives...?﴾ [al-Tahrim: 1].

And He said: ﴿He frowned and turned away, * Because the blind man came to him﴾ [Abasa: 1-2]. Did the Messenger of God (ﷺ) disdain that his Lord corrected him? No, he did not disdain it, as is shown by the fact that he, peace and blessings be upon him, is the one who conveyed this correction and told us of it; and I do not report except what contains honour for me.

This verse gives us a scene from the story of Prophet Sulayman (peace be upon him and our Prophet). Sulayman's story contains many scenes, each of which represents a lesson, an admonition, and a stance of Sulayman in the matter of his call. The first scene in the story concerns his father Dawud (peace be upon him), when he judged in the matter of *al-harth* (the tilth), meaning the crops. The crops belonged to one man, and the sheep of another man came and ate the crops. Almighty Allah has related to us the story of the judgment that Dawud gave, and the matter on which the judgment ended, in the form of a correction to Dawud's ruling from the words of his son Sulayman.

Allah confirmed both rulings, and He said, Glorified is He: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field when the sheep of a people had grazed therein by night, and We were witness to their judgment. And We gave understanding of it to Solomon, and to each We gave judgment and knowledge...﴾ [al-Anbiya: 78-79].

The meaning of ﴿had grazed therein﴾ [al-Anbiya: 78] is that the sheep spread into it and ate it. When the matter was presented to Dawud, he ruled that the owner of the crops should take the sheep.

When Sulayman learned of this ruling, he rejected it and said: "Rather, we should give the land to the owner of the sheep to cultivate until it returns to what it was, and give the sheep to the owner of the land to benefit from them. Then each right returns to its owner." It is as if Allah inspired Sulayman with the correctness of the ruling so that he could correct his father Dawud. So observe how the sanctity of the word of heaven coexisted with the word of the people of the earth. After that, Allah confirmed both rulings and said: ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge...﴾ [al-Anbiya: 79].

Therefore, the correction of one body by another that has ruled is not a defect in the first. Rather, each understood and ruled according to what it understood, and another understood differently and ruled according to that. This is why in the courts we find the initial ruling, the appellate ruling, and after that the ruling of cassation (*naqd*, annulment). Does the appellate ruling impugn the initial ruling, or does the cassation ruling impugn the appellate ruling? No, because the higher ruling takes into account something that escaped the lower judge, so there is no fault in this.

When we review the story, we find that the commentators have not shown us the argument of Dawud in the ruling he issued, nor the argument of Sulayman in the ruling he issued. By inference, we say: in ancient times, crops were not in a demarcated land owned by people. Rather, the land was held in common (*mushaa*). Wherever one sowed the grain and the sky watered it until it bore fruit, one took its fruit without owning the land. That is, whoever reached any field first planted it.

Therefore, ownership belonged to the crop alone and not to the land. On this basis Dawud's ruling was established, and since the land was not owned by the owner of the crops, the matter was crops and sheep. As for Sulayman, he saw that planting represents, as we say, placing a hand on the land, and that placing a hand confers ownership. So he left the owner of the land in possession of his land, and ruled that the owner of the land should take the sheep to benefit from them, and the owner of the sheep should take the land to cultivate it until it returned to what it was, after which each would take what belonged to him.

Therefore, each of them had a point of view, and on this basis he ruled accordingly. Thus Almighty Allah said concerning both of them: ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge...﴾ [al-Anbiya: 79].

The other scene is the trial (*fitnah*) that befell Sulayman. We have said that the original meaning of the word *fitnah* is the smelting of metal and its burning in fire so that the dross and impurities come out of it, and it becomes pure and its hardness increases. Then the word *fitnah* was applied to any test that distinguishes the good from the bad among humans, so it means trial (*ibtila'*).

If you look at *fitnah*, you will find it common among all of Allah's creation. Every one of creation is both a tester and one tested. That is, the rich is a trial for the poor, and the poor is a trial and test for the rich. The rich is tested by the poor: does he withhold blessing from him or give him some of it? Does he despise him for his poverty or respect the decree of Allah concerning him?

Likewise, the poor is tested by the rich: does he envy him for his wealth and object to the decree of Allah with his poverty, or does he endure patiently and wish increase for others? The same applies to the strong and the weak, the healthy and the sick, the ignorant and the learned, and so on. Therefore, each of us is both a tester and one tested. The important question is: who succeeds, and who passes this trial?

Almighty Allah explained this meaning in His saying: ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others...﴾ [al-Furqan: 20]. They said: the word *ba'd* (some) here is not a specification of a particular person. Rather, it is a part of an equal whole, but indefinite within it, as in His saying: ﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service...﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32].

So which of us is raised and which is raised over? They said: each of us is raised in one thing and raised over in another. Thus all people are equal. You have a field in which you excel and show creativity, so you are raised in that field. And you have another field in which you are not skilled and know nothing, so someone else is raised over you in it, because he excels at what you do not.

This matter arises from the distribution of gifts among creation, because they are all servants of Allah, and none of them is a son of Allah, nor is anyone related to Allah by kinship or lineage. Therefore Almighty Allah scattered His bounty upon all His servants and distributed gifts among them equally, for if Allah had made one person the gatherer of all good and virtues, no one would have needed anyone else.

Allah wants His servants to link their hands and cooperate in the movement of life. The strong needs the weak, and the weak needs the strong; the scholar needs the ignorant, and the ignorant needs the learned. Thus people are bound together by need, not by condescension.

We previously explained this matter with the example of the pasha or great man who returns from his work and finds the drains of his house blocked and smells a foul odor in his home, so he hastens to the drain worker to resolve the situation. Perhaps he gets into his car and goes to him at his workplace, and even begs him to come with him. In this case the worker is raised, and the pasha is raised over.

I recall that in our town of Mit Ghamr, in (al-Bursa), there was a café called (Baba). The workers there staged a revolt and said: it is not right for the worker to serve others, nor for him to shine the shoes of people. Why, people? They said: because that is humiliation and degradation. We said to them: then we will shine for ourselves. Indeed, we staged a strike, and each of us bought a tin of polish and began to shine his own shoe. After a while, these men came to al-Bursa complaining of unemployment and scarcity of sustenance, and went about begging people to return to what they had been.

After that we debated with them. One of the brothers said to one of them: "By God, when you ask me a question and I answer it, do I take a fee from you for the answer?" He said: "No." "If you knew how much this answer cost me of my life, my effort, my striving, and my family's toil in raising me, you would know that at that time I was at your service just as you are now at mine. But you looked at us in our time of rest, and you looked at yourselves in your time of work." So: the division is equal, and each of us is at the service of the other, and there is no humiliation or degradation in this. Rather, it is interdependence in the movement of life.

Therefore, after this, Almighty Allah said: ﴿Will you be patient?﴾ [al-Furqan: 20], meaning: will you endure the trial of some of you by others? Even the messengers were tested by the disbelievers, who harmed and oppressed them, and the disbelievers were tested by the messengers.

So among the blessings is that Almighty Allah distributed gifts throughout the universe, and distributed His bounty among creation: ﴿Those who have been given more provision do not return their provision to those whom their right hands possess, so that they are equal therein...﴾ [al-Nahl: 71].

Let us return to Prophet Sulayman and say: what do we know, perhaps kingship and prophethood together enticed Sulayman, so he found something of that in himself. Allah wanted to correct his inner thoughts, because He wanted him for a task higher than what he was in now. Therefore he went through this experience, and found himself on his throne as a body unable to move.

Therefore, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was always mindful of good manners with his Lord and with creation. He (ﷺ) said: [...]. The meaning of this is that prophets may be touched by something and may be tested, but the trial comes from Allah who sent them, and the trial is a correction of the course of the one tested, not a hatred of him, God forbid. Likewise Allah tested Prophet Sulayman, because He was preparing him for a matter more exalted than this. He is a king in outward appearance, but his Lord wants to prepare him to give him something of the dominion (*malakut*).

When Sulayman (peace be upon him) returned and turned in repentance to his Lord, he said: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will not belong to anyone after me; indeed You are the Bestower﴾ [Sad: 35], meaning: he sought forgiveness from his Lord for the delusion he had fallen into. That is: "My Lord, forgive me for what caused You to make me a body." It is as if he said: "O Lord, You tested me with kingship and prophethood, and this is a matter that has not happened to anyone before me, so I became deluded by it. So grant me a kingdom greater than it that will not belong to anyone after me, and I will fulfill this time and not be deluded." It is as if he said to his Lord: "O Lord, test me and give me another chance." When Sulayman made this supplication, his Lord responded to him and gave him what he asked for.

Therefore, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) honored the supplication of his brother Sulayman. It has been reported in the noble hadith [...]. The meaning of ﴿al-Wahhab﴾ [Sad: 35] is an intensive form, indicating abundance of giving. We have said that gift (*hibah*) is giving without return. The meaning is that among what You grant, O Lord, is kingship. This means that kingship is not attained by anyone through his own effort and skill, but is a gift from Allah. Allah is the One who gives kingship, and He gave it even to the disbeliever who argued with Abraham about his Lord, as He said: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, because Allah had given him kingship...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258].

And He said: ﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You remove sovereignty from whom You will...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26].

Almighty God says: "So We subjected the wind to him, flowing gently by his command, wherever he directed" [Sad: 36]. The subjecting of the wind to Solomon was the first blessing added to his kingdom that had not existed before. The meaning of "gentle" (rukhaa') is soft and smooth, like a riding beast that carries its rider at a calm pace, neither disturbing nor throwing him off. However, some exegetes say that the word "gentle" contradicts the words of God in the same story: "the wind, violent" [al-Anbiya': 81]. We say: it is indeed violent, but in a different situation, because the wind in this story has several uses. If it carries him for recreation, it is gentle and soft; if it is for carrying things, it is violent. Therefore, the aspect of the description is separate.

We have also said that when the wind comes in its singular form, it is for punishment, as in God's words: "And in 'Ad, when We sent upon them the barren wind, which left nothing it came upon without making it like rubble" [adh-Dhariyat: 41-42]. But if it comes in plural form, it is for good, as in: "And We sent the winds fertilizing" [al-Hijr: 22].

It is well known that air is what maintains the balance of things, as evidence: if we were to empty the air from one side of a building, for example, it would collapse on that same side, because the air is what supports it and maintains its balance. So when God wills to destroy with the wind, He brings it from one direction. It is as if the Truthful One (subhanahu) is saying: the wind is supposed to come only in punishment and vengeance, but We have subjected it to Solomon so that it brings nothing but good: "So We subjected the wind to him, flowing gently by his command, wherever he directed" [Sad: 36].

His words "wherever he directed" [Sad: 36] mean wherever he intended and wherever he went.

This means that Solomon addressed the wind, which has no language, but God gave him understanding of it. It was as if he became a commander and the wind became one commanded. Thus the wind understood him. God has given each kind of creature its own language through which it communicates with its own kind. When God grants a person understanding of this language, he understands it and communicates with these kinds of creatures.

Among this is God's saying: "We have been taught the speech of the birds" [an-Naml: 16].

Therefore, they have told us about crocodiles in the upper Nile, and about the harmony and complementarity between them and the birds that feed on the leftovers between the crocodile's teeth. After eating, the crocodile leaves to the dry land and opens its mouth, and the bird comes and pecks between its teeth, cleaning them for it. When the bird senses the approach of a hunter, it makes a special sound that the crocodile recognizes, and it hurries to the water and escapes the hunter. Thus the crocodile is a sustainer of life for the bird, and the bird preserves life for the crocodile. So contemplate the perfect reward, how it exists in the world of birds and animals.

No one reaches the level of understanding birds and animals except one whom God has granted this special quality. God granted this special quality to our master Solomon, and he understood the language of the birds and the language of the ants: "A female ant said, 'O ants, enter your dwellings lest Solomon and his soldiers crush you while they are unaware.' So he smiled, laughing at her speech, and said, 'My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteousness of which You will approve, and admit me by Your mercy into the ranks of Your righteous servants'" [an-Naml: 18-19].

So Solomon understood her, and he sensed that this was a blessing God had singled him out with, which requires gratitude. Likewise, he understood the hoopoe, addressed it, and a dialogue took place between them. The story of the hoopoe with Solomon teaches us that everyone who holds a position of authority must follow up on his subordinates in a way by which the committed can be distinguished from the uncommitted.

Had Solomon not inspected the birds, he would not have known the hoopoe was absent. His words: "What is it that I do not see the hoopoe?" [an-Naml: 20] suggest that he imagined the hoopoe was present, but that what prevented him was that he could not see it; therefore he said: "Or is he among the absent?" [an-Naml: 20], because he looked and did not see it. Then the hoopoe came and said: "I have encompassed [knowledge] that you have not encompassed, and I have come to you from Sheba with certain news. Indeed, I found a woman ruling them, and she has been given of everything, and she has a great throne" [an-Naml: 22-23].

What affected him was that she and her people worshipped the sun instead of God: "I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah, and Satan has made their deeds appealing to them and averted them from the way, so they are not guided" [an-Naml: 24].

This moment in the story teaches us that the one who holds a position of authority does not reject what is said to him by those under his authority in a matter they raise; rather, he waits until he hears from them, respects their opinion, and does not confiscate it. We also learn that the hoopoe knew the matter of monotheism and the matter of faith in God.

Then the hoopoe teaches us that every person must preserve the sustainer of his life, and must always keep it in mind if he wishes to live a dignified life. The sustainer of life comes first before planning and setting goals. We understand this from the hoopoe's words: "[Why should they not] prostrate to Allah, who brings out what is hidden in the heavens and the earth and knows what you conceal and what you declare?" [an-Naml: 25].

But why did he single out what is hidden (al-khab'), that which is concealed beneath the earth? They said: because most of the hoopoe's food is what is hidden in the earth, therefore God gave it a long beak with which it pecks the earth and brings out its food.

As for God's words: "And the devils, every builder and diver" [Sad: 37], meaning: We also subjected to him the devils; among them were the builder, who exerts his effort on dry land and cultivates it, and the diver, who exerts his effort in the sea to extract its precious things. "And others bound together in shackles" [Sad: 38], meaning among the devils, "bound together in shackles" meaning restrained and chained in chains. Al-asfad is the plural of safd, which is a chain.

These are restrained, not free like the builder and the diver. But why did God restrain these and free those? They said: because among them are the righteous and obedient, and among them are the disobedient who rebelled against God's method, and it is possible that they also rebel against the Messenger of God. These are the ones who are bound with chains. So the righteous serve him through guidance of faith, and the non-righteous serve him through the guidance of restraints and chains; that is, these by desire and those by fear.

Then He says: "This is Our gift, so grant [favor] or withhold, without account" [Sad: 39]. The gift fits Solomon's request when he asked God for a kingdom that would not be fitting for anyone after him; he said: "Indeed, You are the Bestower" [Sad: 35]. So God replied: "This is Our gift" [Sad: 39]. Since I have bestowed it upon you, I will make you dispose of what I have given you, because I have entrusted you with it: "So grant [favor] or withhold, without account" [Sad: 39], meaning: you are free to give or to withhold and prevent.

The Truthful One did not grant Solomon unrestricted freedom of disposal except because He ensured from him justice in disposal, for Solomon, when he asked for the vast kingdom, pledged to God this justice. Therefore they said about him, peace be upon him, that he used to eat only the coarse bran of grain, that is the husk or chaff, and leave the pure flour for the slaves and the common people.

It is as if he did not seek the blessing and vast kingdom in order to enjoy it himself or to show off; rather, he sought it to employ it in serving the call to God, and because he was going to confront a power that was the greatest of powers at that time. It is sufficient that God described this power with His words: "And she has a great throne" [an-Naml: 23], that is, Bilqis.

Here, in this confrontation, the effect and value of kingship will appear. When Bilqis tempted him with wealth, he said: "Do you provide me with wealth? What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you. Rather, you are proud of your gift" [an-Naml: 36].

Here the wisdom appears in that Solomon, when he asked for a kingdom that would not be fitting for anyone after him, sought it so that no one would be superior to him, and so that no one would try to tempt, bribe, or win him over with money, as Bilqis tried with her vast kingdom in prosperous Yemen at that time.

What indicated Bilqis's sagacity in this situation is that she consulted the notables and nobles of the people and those of judgment among them: "She said, 'O eminent ones, indeed there has been delivered to me a noble letter. Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed it says: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful'" [an-Naml: 29-30].

First: how did she know it was a noble letter? They said: because she found it in her chamber without a messenger bringing it or anyone entering with it, and no guards prevented it, and it did not require her permission to enter. Therefore she knew it came from a higher source than hers, and the movement of the letter's owner in life must be stronger than hers, as evidenced by the fact that the letter reached her in this manner. Therefore she consulted the people: "I have never decided a matter until you have borne witness to me" [an-Naml: 32].

The story ended with her saying: "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds" [an-Naml: 44].

So His words "This is Our gift, so grant or withhold, without account" [Sad: 39] indicate that God's gift to the prophets is not for vanity and boasting, but a gift for the servants of God's call. Therefore we see that those whom God made to possess some keys of the unseen did not exploit their knowledge of the unseen for their own benefit, and miracles may occur at their hands or through their tongues while they are unaware of them, and charismatic gifts (karamat) appear from them while they themselves do not recognize or perceive them.

That is because God's secret was given to them, not so that they would exalt themselves over people, but so that they would increase in servitude and in the path of servitude to God, and so that they would be models for guiding creation and taking them by the hand to the path of truth.

It is related that our master 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, when rain was withheld and the land became barren, went out to seek rain, and brought out the weak among the children, the elderly, and the women, until he brought out the animals, as if saying: "O Lord, if You have withheld rain from us because of our sins, then give us drink for the sake of these." But the sky did not rain, and 'Umar prepared to turn back. While he was returning, he found a slave standing among the rocks, raising his hands and gazing at the sky. 'Umar said: "By Allah, he had not lowered his hands before the sky rained like the mouths of waterskins."

Then 'Umar was amazed how the sky had not responded to him but responded to this slave. 'Umar looked at the slave's face until he recognized him, and went to the slave-dealer and said: "Show me your slaves." The dealer thought he wanted to buy, so he displayed the best he had of men with rippling muscles and sound build, but 'Umar did not turn to any of them. The man said: "By Allah, I have nothing but this slave, and he is a burden on his master; wherever he goes he brings no good."

When the slave came, 'Umar recognized him and said: "Is this you?" The slave looked at him, raised his gaze to the sky, and said: "O Allah, as You have exposed me among Your creation, then take me without temptation," and he went on his way. This is the state of one in whom saintliness (wilaya) and charisma (karama) appear: he does not desire them nor love that they be revealed before people; he does not want them, and God's affection for him through them is sufficient.
