Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed it says: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful'" [an-Naml: 29-30].

First: how did she know it was a noble letter? They said: because she found it in her chamber without a messenger bringing it or anyone entering with it, and no guards prevented it, and it did not require her permission to enter. Therefore she knew it came from a higher source than hers, and the movement of the letter's owner in life must be stronger than hers, as evidenced by the fact that the letter reached her in this manner. Therefore she consulted the people: "I have never decided a matter until you have borne witness to me" [an-Naml: 32].

The story ended with her saying: "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds" [an-Naml: 44].

So His words "This is Our gift, so grant or withhold, without account" [Sad: 39] indicate that God's gift to the prophets is not for vanity and boasting, but a gift for the servants of God's call. Therefore we see that those whom God made to possess some keys of the unseen did not exploit their knowledge of the unseen for their own benefit, and miracles may occur at their hands or through their tongues while they are unaware of them, and charismatic gifts (karamat) appear from them while they themselves do not recognize or perceive them.

That is because God's secret was given to them, not so that they would exalt themselves over people, but so that they would increase in servitude and in the path of servitude to God, and so that they would be models for guiding creation and taking them by the hand to the path of truth.

It is related that our master 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, when rain was withheld and the land became barren, went out to seek rain, and brought out the weak among the children, the elderly, and the women, until he brought out the animals, as if saying: "O Lord, if You have withheld rain from us because of our sins, then give us drink for the sake of these." But the sky did not rain, and 'Umar prepared to turn back. While he was returning, he found a slave standing among the rocks, raising his hands and gazing at the sky. 'Umar said: "By Allah, he had not lowered his hands before the sky rained like the mouths of waterskins."

Then 'Umar was amazed how the sky had not responded to him but responded to this slave. 'Umar looked at the slave's face until he recognized him, and went to the slave-dealer and said: "Show me your slaves." The dealer thought he wanted to buy, so he displayed the best he had of men with rippling muscles and sound build, but 'Umar did not turn to any of them. The man said: "By Allah, I have nothing but this slave, and he is a burden on his master; wherever he goes he brings no good."

When the slave came, 'Umar recognized him and said: "Is this you?" The slave looked at him, raised his gaze to the sky, and said: "O Allah, as You have exposed me among Your creation, then take me without temptation," and he went on his way. This is the state of one in whom saintliness (wilaya) and charisma (karama) appear: he does not desire them nor love that they be revealed before people; he does not want them, and God's affection for him through them is sufficient.

Almighty God says: "So We subjected the wind to him, flowing gently by his command, wherever he directed" [Sad: 36]. The subjecting of the wind to Solomon was the first blessing added to his kingdom that had not existed before. The meaning of "gentle" (rukhaa') is soft and smooth, like a riding beast that carries its rider at a calm pace, neither disturbing nor throwing him off. However, some exegetes say that the word "gentle" contradicts the words of God in the same story: "the wind, violent" [al-Anbiya': 81]. We say: it is indeed violent, but in a different situation, because the wind in this story has several uses. If it carries him for recreation, it is gentle and soft; if it is for carrying things, it is violent. Therefore, the aspect of the description is separate.

We have also said that when the wind comes in its singular form, it is for punishment, as in God's words: "And in 'Ad, when We sent upon them the barren wind, which left nothing it came upon without making it like rubble" [adh-Dhariyat: 41-42]. But if it comes in plural form, it is for good, as in: "And We sent the winds fertilizing" [al-Hijr: 22].

It is well known that air is what maintains the balance of things, as evidence: if we were to empty the air from one side of a building, for example, it would collapse on that same side, because the air is what supports it and maintains its balance. So when God wills to destroy with the wind, He brings it from one direction. It is as if the Truthful One (subhanahu) is saying: the wind is supposed to come only in punishment and vengeance, but We have subjected it to Solomon so that it brings nothing but good: "So We subjected the wind to him, flowing gently by his command, wherever he directed" [Sad: 36].

His words "wherever he directed" [Sad: 36] mean wherever he intended and wherever he went.

This means that Solomon addressed the wind, which has no language, but God gave him understanding of it. It was as if he became a commander and the wind became one commanded. Thus the wind understood him. God has given each kind of creature its own language through which it communicates with its own kind. When God grants a person understanding of this language, he understands it and communicates with these kinds of creatures.

Among this is God's saying: "We have been taught the speech of the birds" [an-Naml: 16].

Therefore, they have told us about crocodiles in the upper Nile, and about the harmony and complementarity between them and the birds that feed on the leftovers between the crocodile's teeth. After eating, the crocodile leaves to the dry land and opens its mouth, and the bird comes and pecks between its teeth, cleaning them for it. When the bird senses the approach of a hunter, it makes a special sound that the crocodile recognizes, and it hurries to the water and escapes the hunter. Thus the crocodile is a sustainer of life for the bird, and the bird preserves life for the crocodile. So contemplate the perfect reward, how it exists in the world of birds and animals.

No one reaches the level of understanding birds and animals except one whom God has granted this special quality. God granted this special quality to our master Solomon, and he understood the language of the birds and the language of the ants: "A female ant said, 'O ants, enter your dwellings lest Solomon and his soldiers crush you while they are unaware.' So he smiled, laughing at her speech, and said, 'My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteousness of which You will approve, and admit me by Your mercy into the ranks of Your righteous servants'" [an-Naml: 18-19].

So Solomon understood her, and he sensed that this was a blessing God had singled him out with, which requires gratitude. Likewise, he understood the hoopoe, addressed it, and a dialogue took place between them. The story of the hoopoe with Solomon teaches us that everyone who holds a position of authority must follow up on his subordinates in a way by which the committed can be distinguished from the uncommitted.

Had Solomon not inspected the birds, he would not have known the hoopoe was absent. His words: "What is it that I do not see the hoopoe?" [an-Naml: 20] suggest that he imagined the hoopoe was present, but that what prevented him was that he could not see it; therefore he said: "Or is he among the absent?" [an-Naml: 20], because he looked and did not see it. Then the hoopoe came and said: "I have encompassed [knowledge] that you have not encompassed, and I have come to you from Sheba with certain news. Indeed, I found a woman ruling them, and she has been given of everything, and she has a great throne" [an-Naml: 22-23].

What affected him was that she and her people worshipped the sun instead of God: "I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah, and Satan has made their deeds appealing to them and averted them from the way, so they are not guided" [an-Naml: 24].

This moment in the story teaches us that the one who holds a position of authority does not reject what is said to him by those under his authority in a matter they raise; rather, he waits until he hears from them, respects their opinion, and does not confiscate it. We also learn that the hoopoe knew the matter of monotheism and the matter of faith in God.

Then the hoopoe teaches us that every person must preserve the sustainer of his life, and must always keep it in mind if he wishes to live a dignified life. The sustainer of life comes first before planning and setting goals. We understand this from the hoopoe's words: "[Why should they not] prostrate to Allah, who brings out what is hidden in the heavens and the earth and knows what you conceal and what you declare?" [an-Naml: 25].

But why did he single out what is hidden (al-khab'), that which is concealed beneath the earth? They said: because most of the hoopoe's food is what is hidden in the earth, therefore God gave it a long beak with which it pecks the earth and brings out its food.

As for God's words: "And the devils, every builder and diver" [Sad: 37], meaning: We also subjected to him the devils; among them were the builder, who exerts his effort on dry land and cultivates it, and the diver, who exerts his effort in the sea to extract its precious things. "And others bound together in shackles" [Sad: 38], meaning among the devils, "bound together in shackles" meaning restrained and chained in chains. Al-asfad is the plural of safd, which is a chain.

These are restrained, not free like the builder and the diver. But why did God restrain these and free those? They said: because among them are the righteous and obedient, and among them are the disobedient who rebelled against God's method, and it is possible that they also rebel against the Messenger of God. These are the ones who are bound with chains. So the righteous serve him through guidance of faith, and the non-righteous serve him through the guidance of restraints and chains; that is, these by desire and those by fear.

Then He says: "This is Our gift, so grant [favor] or withhold, without account" [Sad: 39]. The gift fits Solomon's request when he asked God for a kingdom that would not be fitting for anyone after him; he said: "Indeed, You are the Bestower" [Sad: 35]. So God replied: "This is Our gift" [Sad: 39]. Since I have bestowed it upon you, I will make you dispose of what I have given you, because I have entrusted you with it: "So grant [favor] or withhold, without account" [Sad: 39], meaning: you are free to give or to withhold and prevent.

The Truthful One did not grant Solomon unrestricted freedom of disposal except because He ensured from him justice in disposal, for Solomon, when he asked for the vast kingdom, pledged to God this justice. Therefore they said about him, peace be upon him, that he used to eat only the coarse bran of grain, that is the husk or chaff, and leave the pure flour for the slaves and the common people.

It is as if he did not seek the blessing and vast kingdom in order to enjoy it himself or to show off; rather, he sought it to employ it in serving the call to God, and because he was going to confront a power that was the greatest of powers at that time. It is sufficient that God described this power with His words: "And she has a great throne" [an-Naml: 23], that is, Bilqis.

Here, in this confrontation, the effect and value of kingship will appear. When Bilqis tempted him with wealth, he said: "Do you provide me with wealth? What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you. Rather, you are proud of your gift" [an-Naml: 36].

Here the wisdom appears in that Solomon, when he asked for a kingdom that would not be fitting for anyone after him, sought it so that no one would be superior to him, and so that no one would try to tempt, bribe, or win him over with money, as Bilqis tried with her vast kingdom in prosperous Yemen at that time.

Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed it says: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful'" [an-Naml: 29-30].

The story ended with her saying: "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds" [an-Naml: 44].

That is because God's secret was given to them, not so that they would exalt themselves over people, but so that they would increase in servitude and in the path of servitude to God, and so that they would be models for guiding creation and taking them by the hand to the path of truth.

...fa-mnun aw amsik bi-ghayri hisab, meaning: you are free to give or to withhold and restrain.

And Allah, glory be to Him, did not grant Solomon unrestricted freedom of disposal except because He had guaranteed from him justice in disposal, for when Solomon asked for a vast kingdom, he pledged to Allah, exalted is He, this justice...

So it is as if he did not seek blessing and a vast kingdom in order to enjoy it himself, or to boast, but rather he sought it to subject it to the service of calling to Allah. And because he would confront a power that was the greatest of powers at that time, and it suffices that Allah, exalted is He, described this power in His saying: ﴿And she has a mighty throne﴾ [al-Naml: 23], meaning Bilqis...

(Lazulfa) means nearness, that is, closeness (to Allah). What indicates this nearness is that Allah the Exalted gave him a kingdom that is not suitable for anyone after him, and gave him freedom to dispose of this kingdom: He gives to whom He wills and withholds from whom He wills. Allah granted him this gift in return for His knowledge that he would not use it for tyranny, nor for arrogance, nor for lording it over people; rather, he would place it in the position that Allah wills for it. Thus he became trusted with Allah's gift.

The meaning of ﴿وَحُسْنَ مَآبٍ﴾ [Sad: 40] is: a good return and a good place of coming back to Allah on the Day of Resurrection.

Then the context moves us on to the story of another prophet, our master Ayyub (peace be upon him):

﴿And remember Our servant Ayyub...﴾.

And remember Our servant Job, when he called upon his Lord: "Indeed, Satan has touched me with hardship and torment." (38:41)

The description of him as a servant ('abd) is here an honour, because it shows the Lord's exaltation of the rank of servanthood ('ubudiyya). We have said that servanthood is a despised word among people, because servitude to other humans is humiliation and subjugation, in which the master takes the best of his servant and the fruit of his effort in life. But servanthood to God Most High is a beloved description and a praiseworthy word, because the servant in it takes the best of his Master.

Therefore, when God Most High bestowed His favour upon our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), in the event of the Night Journey and the Ascension (al-Isra' wa'l-Mi'raj), He made the basis of that servanthood to Him, Glorified is He, saying: "Glory be to Him who took His servant by night..." (17:1). When the hospitality of the earth became narrow for him at al-Ta'if, his Lord wished to show him the hospitality of the heavens. The quality that raised Muhammad to this station is his sincerity in servanthood to his Lord.

As for the meaning of "Satan has touched me with hardship and torment" (38:41): al-mass (touch) is a gentle, light contact, meaning less than al-lams (touching). They said: he had fallen ill with a severe sickness that affected his skin, and Satan kept hovering around him with evil thoughts, saying to him: "How can God do this to you, when you are a Messenger? How can He leave you like this without healing you?"

Thus there gathered upon our master Job the pain of the skin and bodily torment, together with the whisperings of Satan in his inner thoughts. Therefore he said: "with hardship (nusb) and torment." Nusb with a ḍamma is like nasab with a fatha, and al-nassab means fatigue; they are like bukhl and bakhl, both meaning the same thing.

They said regarding the touch of Satan: the action in truth belongs to God Most High; God is the One who acts, and Satan, by his whispering, is a means, while God Most High is the Causer. So the touch of Satan means his whispering, which occupied the mind of our master Job. It is as if the Truth, Glorified is He, wished Job to take heed that this whispering should not have been allowed to pass through his mind.

When sickness and the whisperings of Satan gathered upon our master Job, he became weak, so he turned to his Lord, calling upon Him to cut off from him the whisperings of Satan, because they need repelling, and repelling needs strength, and his strength was bound to his illness. Therefore he prayed to God so that his weakness would not increase through Satan's whispering. When he called upon God, God responded to him:

﴿Strike with your foot; here is a cool place to wash and a drink...﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 38, verse 42:

... It is as if the Truth, glory be to Him, is saying to him: "I do not test you out of dislike for you, nor as a hardship upon you. Rather, I wish to hear from you that you dislike whatever comes into your mind that distances you from Me." ﴿Strike with your foot﴾... That is: the matter is easy and simple for Me, just as you say: "O so-and-so, the matter is trivial, it is beneath your feet."

Al-rakd (striking) is to propel forcefully and swiftly. You say: "I struck the horse" (rakadtu al-faras), meaning: I pressed it with my leg, like this, from beneath, so that it would hasten. Then the context passes over the matter of striking directly to the result: ﴿This is a cool bath and a drink﴾, and does not say: "So he struck, and water gushed forth, and so-and-so." Rather, all of that is folded up, and the command ﴿Strike﴾ suffices.

The meaning is: in this water there is a bath for you and a drink, because the illness that afflicted our master Ayyub (peace be upon him) appears to have been a skin disease that leaves pustules on the skin, disfiguring it. Today we see doctors who treat skin diseases using topical ointments that treat the surface of the disease, but do not reach the internal cause of the disease.

So it was among God's mercy toward our master Ayyub that He made his cure, both outward and inward, in a single strike that brings forth water, whereby he bathes in a cool bath that heals the surface of his illness, and a drink that heals the causes of the disease within his body.

God says: ﴿And We gave him his family﴾. It seems that some of his family had withdrawn from him when the illness struck him, and when God healed him and he returned to a state of well-being, they came back to him. ﴿And the like of them with them﴾: that is, We gave him the like of his family, meaning of offspring and followers. ﴿As a mercy from Us and a reminder for people of understanding.﴾ The reminder (dhikra) is the thought that passes through you to turn you toward the object of remembrance, because you are in the midst of something that distances you from the cause of remembrance.

The content of the reminder here is that when he was patient, relief came to him from God. His body returned healthy and sound after he was cured of the illness and of its causes, and then his family came back to him, with their number doubled, out of tenderness toward his feelings. This is what is meant by the mercy in God's words ﴿as a mercy from Us﴾. These are multiple gifts that came as the fruit and result of his patience, peace be upon him, and his contentment with what God decreed.

So the reminder we take from this story is that when a person is struck by distress, he turns to God and seeks refuge in Him in his affliction.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 38, verse 44:

Al-ḍigh th (al-ḍighth): a bundle of grass, or a bundle of palm-spathe fronds (shamārīkh al-balah, the stalks of dates).

His saying ﴿And take in your hand a bundle and strike with it, and do not break your oath⟩ [Ṣād 38:44] indicates that there was an oath in the matter, which God wished Ayyūb not to break. This verse draws our attention to a story which the Sunnah has explained. They said: the Devil went to one of the wives of our master Ayyūb and said to her: "Ask Ayyūb to seek refuge with me, and I will cure him immediately, on condition that he says: 'It was the Devil who cured me.'" Since she was eager for him to be healed, she said to him: "By God, a thought came to me and told me such-and-such." He said: "It is the Devil. You listened to him, and you want me to obey him? By God, besides whom there is no god, I will surely flog you one hundred times." This is the oath which God wished Ayyūb not to break, so He said to him: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle and strike with it, and do not break your oath⟩ [Ṣād 38:44].

The Prophet (ﷺ) did something similar when the man al-Aḥbann came to him. Aḥbann, from (ḥ b n), means one with a large belly, or one who has dropsy (istisqā'). He had committed fornication with a frail, sick woman. When he confessed his crime, the Messenger (ﷺ) feared that he would die if the prescribed punishment (ḥadd) were carried out on him, so he commanded that he be struck with a bundle of grass, or a hundred palm-frond stalks, struck with them once at one time.

The meaning of ﴿strike with it⟩ [Ṣād 38:44] is: strike with it the one whom you swore to flog, ﴿and do not break your oath⟩ [Ṣād 38:44], meaning in your oath. ﴿Indeed, We found him patient⟩ [Ṣād 38:44]. This relief is thus a reward for his patience and for his turning back to his Lord. God gave him something that pleases him, by lightening for him even the pain which would fall upon others, since he had sworn to flog her; it would have been necessary for him to flog her in reality so that he would not break his oath, but God lightened it for him so that it would not hurt his family.

(واذكر) i.e., with praise and commendation, (Our servants) plural of servant. We have said that servitude is loathed if it is toward humans, but servitude to God is honor and nobility. (Abraham) is the father of the prophets. (Isaac) God gave him to Abraham after Abraham submitted the judgment to God when He commanded him to slaughter his son Ishmael. (Jacob) is the son of Isaac.

We have already stood on the story of these prophets in the words of the Exalted, on the tongue of Abraham saying to his son Ishmael: ﴿O my dear son, indeed I have seen in a dream that I am slaughtering you, so see what you think...﴾ [al-Saffat: 102]. Abraham did not wish to proceed to slaughter his son before explaining to him the matter that had been issued to him, because he feared that he might take him by surprise, and the son's heart would fill with resentment toward his father, since he would not know the wisdom behind his father killing him. Then he wished to make his son share with him in submission to God, and not to deprive him of the reward.

Therefore the Exalted said: ﴿So when they had both submitted...﴾ [al-Saffat: 103], meaning Abraham and Ishmael, ﴿and he put him down upon his forehead. And We called to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, We thus reward the doers of good. Indeed, this is the clear test. And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice. And We left for him among later generations: "Peace upon Abraham." Thus do We reward the doers of good. Indeed, he was among Our believing servants. And We gave him good tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous. And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are doers of good and those who clearly wrong themselves.﴾ [al-Saffat: 103–113].

So: Isaac came, and after him Jacob came, as a result of Abraham's submission and compliance with his Lord's command to slaughter Ishmael. He spared Ishmael, and God granted Isaac and Jacob as an increase and bounty from Him, because the Truthful, glorified is He, does not desire by trial to punish people.

Therefore we have said: Our master Abraham has a virtue over every Muslim, and a favor upon the neck of every believer. Why? Because if the slaughter had been carried out on Ishmael, it would have become a trial from God for humans, that they draw near to God by slaughtering their son. But our master Abraham, by his faith and by submitting the matter and judgment to God, bore this burden on our behalf, and lifted this ruling from us. Otherwise, it would have become a rite and a worship obligatory upon every believer after him. The poet spoke truly:

Submit to your Lord's judgment, for in His wisdom He decrees it, until you find rest and gain.

Remember the Friend of God in the slaughter of his son, when his Creator said, and when they both submitted.

We learn from this matter that every affair or event that harms a person in its outward appearance and tires him, which a person regards as a calamity, should not be looked at in isolation from its doer; rather, one must take the event together with the one who caused it, because the judgment on an event changes when viewed in relation to the agent.

We clarified this matter and said: Suppose your son came in to you with blood flowing from his face. Then you are not concerned with the injury as much as you are concerned with the perpetrator. The first question you ask is: Who did this to you? Then you wait to hear the name of the doer. If the boy says, "My uncle hit me," you will calm down and say: You must have done something that made your uncle deserve to hit you. But if he tells you, "So-and-so," especially if he is your enemy, you will raise the world and not let it rest.

Therefore: one cannot judge an act as good or evil except by attributing it to its doer, because by attributing the act to an agent, its goodness or evil becomes clear.

The meaning of ﴿owners of hands and sight﴾ [Sad: 45]: owners of hands, hands being the plural of hand. The word "hand" is used for the known bodily organ, and it is also used for what the organ produces of action. You say, "So-and-so has a hand upon me," meaning favor and kindness. And because most actions are carried out by the hand, the blessing that reaches someone through the hand was named after this acting organ. Among this is the saying of the poet:

He has enduring favors upon me, which I count but cannot count all of them.

There is a difference between the active movement that performs the act and another meaning of active movement, which is what obligates you to move. For example, when we want to give and bestow: whoever has wealth gives with his hand, whereas the destitute does not give, but advises the one who has wealth to spend from it.

The Exalted says: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick, nor upon those who find nothing to spend, when they are sincere to God and His Messenger. There is no path against the doers of good...﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91].

So the work here is not with the hand but with the tongue. But since the hand is the instrument with which most works are performed, we attribute every good that extends from you to others to the hand; therefore the Exalted says: ﴿The hand of God is above their hands...﴾ [al-Fath: 10].

If a person does not have wealth, and is unable to advise with the tongue, God the Exalted never deprives him of righteous action in giving, and He is satisfied from him that he rejoices in the one who gives and is pleased by the giving of others.

An example of this: a man was heard praying at the Ka'bah saying: "O God, You know that I disobey You, but I love those who obey You." And al-Asma'i heard a man at al-Multazam praying and saying: "O Lord, I know that I disobey You, and I am ashamed to ask You while I disobey You, but there is no god but You, so to whom shall I go?" Then he said to him: "O man, your Lord forgives you for the goodness of your request."

It is well known that the believer strives in supplication, especially at al-Multazam, and tries to make his supplication and request good in this situation.

Another rank God grants to one who does not find [wealth], so that he is not deprived of reward in giving, is that he grieves because he has nothing to give, as in the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿Nor upon those who came to you that you might provide them mounts, and you said, "I find nothing upon which to carry you," they turned away while their eyes overflowed with tears of grief that they did not find what they could spend.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 92].

So the Truthful, glorified is He, does not deprive a believer of having a position in giving, even if it is a passive giving.

Among the meanings of hand is strength, as in the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿The hand of God is above their hands...﴾ [al-Fath: 10]. So the intended meaning of ﴿owners of hands...﴾ [Sad: 45] is: owners of strength in obedience to God.

And ﴿sight﴾ [Sad: 45]: meaning insights in knowledge, religion and wisdom. As for sight in the sense of the faculty of seeing, it is present in all, believer and non-believer alike. So the intended sight is that which sees and then performs another task beyond sight, adding light upon light.

Thus sight alone is not sufficient, because the signs of God in the cosmos are the given data, as we say in a mathematical problem; and these data need a conscious insight to bring the data to the required result, which is faith in the One who gave these data.

So when sights look at the cosmos, see its data, and see God's signs in it, and then are not affected intellectually or emotionally by them, and do not turn to its Maker and Originator, then these sights have no value.

Thus the meaning of ﴿sight﴾ [Sad: 45] is: owners of insights that occupied minds and emotions with what they see of signs, and who knew that this cosmos can only be attributed to a powerful, manifest, dominant force with no partner. For if it had a partner, its effect would have appeared, and he would have defended his right to this dominion. Since no opponent has appeared and no one has claimed to have created it, the matter belongs to the one who asserts it.

Therefore the Exalted says: ﴿Say: If there were with Him other gods, as they say, they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne.﴾ [al-Isra: 42].

He placed the hands before the sights, because the work of the hands is the final result of sight; for you see the signs of God in His creation and know that He is the Lord of all, the Creator of all, the Provider of all, so your heart softens toward the poor and you give to him, perhaps you will become like him one day and find someone to give you, and you will not harbor resentment toward the wealthy while you are destitute, because the wealthy one's goodness will reach you in any case.

Therefore the Exalted said: ﴿Let those fear who, were they to leave behind them weak offspring, would fear for them. So let them fear God and speak words of rectitude.﴾ [al-Nisa: 9].

And let us take a lesson from His saying: ﴿And their father was righteous...﴾ [al-Kahf: 82].

Then the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, We chose them with a pure quality: the remembrance of the Abode﴾ [Sad: 46].

"We chose them" means: We gave them something pure for them. The "pure quality" with which We singled them out is that which constantly turns them toward the Abode of recompense, which is the Hereafter. Through this remembrance a person remains constantly mindful of the reward of obedience and the punishment of disobedience, and when a person keeps this end in mind, he stays steadfast in obedience and distances himself from disobedience.

Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said in clarifying this matter: Why was faith negated from him in this moment? They said: Because he was heedless of the consequence of his act, heedless of the recompense. Heedlessness is what makes us lazy in obedience, brings us into disobedience, and entices us toward it; and if a person kept the punishment for disobedience in mind, he would not fall into it.

We previously gave an example, saying: Suppose a young man has a sexual craving. We say to him: We will provide what you want, but after you spend your night, we will take you to this blazing furnace and place you in it for one hour. What do you think of such a young man? He will surely flee from this disobedience, run from it, and renounce it. Why? Because he has witnessed the consequence and kept the recompense in mind.

Likewise the student who works hard at his lessons, to the point that he neglects his eating and drinking: why does he do so? Because he keeps in mind the pleasure of success, the honor of excellence, and the high standing among his family and classmates. On the other hand, the negligent student is negligent only because he is heedless of the consequence of negligence and the humiliation of failure on the day its result appears.

So the meaning of ﴿the remembrance of the Abode﴾ [Sad: 46] is: he remains always mindful of it, keeping the reward for obedience in view so that he turns toward it, and keeping the punishment for disobedience in view so that he flees from it.

And His saying: ﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen, the best﴾ [Sad: 47].

That is: those whom We have chosen. God the Exalted has choices in creation: He chooses from places and times what He wills, as He chose the Ka'bah and Bayt al-Maqdis among places, and chose the month of Ramadan among times. Likewise He chooses from humans messengers, and from angels messengers.

Choosing is not a pampering of the chosen nor a favoritism toward him; rather it is entrusting the chosen with what the chooser desires, namely spreading goodness among his kind. The choosing of messengers is not a pampering of them; rather choosing burdens them with great responsibilities in their persons, selves, wealth and families.

Likewise He chose Ramadan not so that we worship and obey God only during Ramadan, but so that obedience spreads through all time, by taking from Ramadan the energy needed for the whole year. Thus the choosing of a time, a place, a person, or angels is not a pampering of one creation over another, but for spreading goodness to all creation for all creation.

The meaning of ﴿the best﴾ [Sad: 47] is the plural of "khayyir" (good). The meaning: We chose them for the goodness in them which qualifies them for this choosing.

(واذكر) i.e., with praise and commendation, (Our servants) plural of servant. We have said that servitude is loathed if it is toward humans, but servitude to God is honor and nobility. (Abraham) is the father of the prophets. (Isaac) God gave him to Abraham after Abraham submitted the judgment to God when He commanded him to slaughter his son Ishmael. (Jacob) is the son of Isaac.

We have already stood on the story of these prophets in the words of the Exalted, on the tongue of Abraham saying to his son Ishmael: ﴿O my dear son, indeed I have seen in a dream that I am slaughtering you, so see what you think...﴾ [al-Saffat: 102]. Abraham did not wish to proceed to slaughter his son before explaining to him the matter that had been issued to him, because he feared that he might take him by surprise, and the son's heart would fill with resentment toward his father, since he would not know the wisdom behind his father killing him. Then he wished to make his son share with him in submission to God, and not to deprive him of the reward.

Therefore the Exalted said: ﴿So when they had both submitted...﴾ [al-Saffat: 103], meaning Abraham and Ishmael, ﴿and he put him down upon his forehead. And We called to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, We thus reward the doers of good. Indeed, this is the clear test. And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice. And We left for him among later generations: "Peace upon Abraham." Thus do We reward the doers of good. Indeed, he was among Our believing servants. And We gave him good tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous. And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are doers of good and those who clearly wrong themselves.﴾ [al-Saffat: 103–113].

So: Isaac came, and after him Jacob came, as a result of Abraham's submission and compliance with his Lord's command to slaughter Ishmael. He spared Ishmael, and God granted Isaac and Jacob as an increase and bounty from Him, because the Truthful, glorified is He, does not desire by trial to punish people.

Therefore we have said: Our master Abraham has a virtue over every Muslim, and a favor upon the neck of every believer. Why? Because if the slaughter had been carried out on Ishmael, it would have become a trial from God for humans, that they draw near to God by slaughtering their son. But our master Abraham, by his faith and by submitting the matter and judgment to God, bore this burden on our behalf, and lifted this ruling from us. Otherwise, it would have become a rite and a worship obligatory upon every believer after him. The poet spoke truly:

Submit to your Lord's judgment, for in His wisdom He decrees it, until you find rest and gain.

Remember the Friend of God in the slaughter of his son, when his Creator said, and when they both submitted.

We learn from this matter that every affair or event that harms a person in its outward appearance and tires him, which a person regards as a calamity, should not be looked at in isolation from its doer; rather, one must take the event together with the one who caused it, because the judgment on an event changes when viewed in relation to the agent.

We clarified this matter and said: Suppose your son came in to you with blood flowing from his face. Then you are not concerned with the injury as much as you are concerned with the perpetrator. The first question you ask is: Who did this to you? Then you wait to hear the name of the doer. If the boy says, "My uncle hit me," you will calm down and say: You must have done something that made your uncle deserve to hit you. But if he tells you, "So-and-so," especially if he is your enemy, you will raise the world and not let it rest.

Therefore: one cannot judge an act as good or evil except by attributing it to its doer, because by attributing the act to an agent, its goodness or evil becomes clear.

The meaning of ﴿owners of hands and sight﴾ [Sad: 45]: owners of hands, hands being the plural of hand. The word "hand" is used for the known bodily organ, and it is also used for what the organ produces of action. You say, "So-and-so has a hand upon me," meaning favor and kindness. And because most actions are carried out by the hand, the blessing that reaches someone through the hand was named after this acting organ. Among this is the saying of the poet:

He has enduring favors upon me, which I count but cannot count all of them.

There is a difference between the active movement that performs the act and another meaning of active movement, which is what obligates you to move. For example, when we want to give and bestow: whoever has wealth gives with his hand, whereas the destitute does not give, but advises the one who has wealth to spend from it.

The Exalted says: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick, nor upon those who find nothing to spend, when they are sincere to God and His Messenger. There is no path against the doers of good...﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91].

So the work here is not with the hand but with the tongue. But since the hand is the instrument with which most works are performed, we attribute every good that extends from you to others to the hand; therefore the Exalted says: ﴿The hand of God is above their hands...﴾ [al-Fath: 10].

If a person does not have wealth, and is unable to advise with the tongue, God the Exalted never deprives him of righteous action in giving, and He is satisfied from him that he rejoices in the one who gives and is pleased by the giving of others.

An example of this: a man was heard praying at the Ka'bah saying: "O God, You know that I disobey You, but I love those who obey You." And al-Asma'i heard a man at al-Multazam praying and saying: "O Lord, I know that I disobey You, and I am ashamed to ask You while I disobey You, but there is no god but You, so to whom shall I go?" Then he said to him: "O man, your Lord forgives you for the goodness of your request."

Election (al-istifa'") is not a pampering of the one chosen, nor a favouring of him. Rather, it is a trust (ta'min) placed upon the chosen one with respect to what the one who chooses (al-mustafi) wants from him: the spreading of good among his kind. Thus the choosing of the messengers is not a pampering of them. Rather, the choosing burdens them with great burdens in their persons and selves, and in their wealth and their families...

The word al-akhyar is the plural of khayyir. The meaning is: We chose them for the goodness that is in them, which qualifies them for this choosing.

Our master Isma'il is known to us all through his story with his father Ibrahim. The scholars differ here about Sayyidna Dhu al-Kifl, because among the messengers are some whom God counted in the procession of the messages, but of whom we are told only their names and attributes. Dhu al-Kifl is mentioned here by this description: ﴿And indeed they are with Us, among the chosen and the excellent﴾ [Sad: 47]. As for al-Yasa', we know nothing about him except his name. The Qur'an does not mention who he was, when he was sent, to whom he was sent, or the method he brought. Likewise, concerning Dhu al-Kifl, the Qur'an mentions only his name, and here he is described as one of the chosen and the excellent. In Surat al-Anbiya', God, glory be to Him, said of him: ﴿And Isma'il, Idris and Dhu al-Kifl, all of them were among the patient. And We admitted them into Our mercy; indeed they were among the righteous﴾ [al-Anbiya': 85-86].

So he is described once as among the excellent, once as among the patient, and once as among the righteous, and for this God admitted him into His mercy. This is what caused the scholars to differ over Dhu al-Kifl: was he a messenger or not? However, the majority of scholars hold that he was a messenger, based on the fact that God placed him among those messengers.

It has been said about Dhu al-Kifl that he lived in the period of al-Yasa' and during al-Yasa's mission. Al-Yasa' wished to appoint a man over the people after him, and wished to see his conduct among the subjects and how this man would behave in the last part of his life. When he saw that his own strength was unable to carry out the task of the call (to God), and from his keenness for the call after him, he wanted to test whoever he would appoint as successor and see what he would do.

When al-Yasa' sat among his people he said: "Who will undertake from me with three [things]?" The preposition *bi* (with), as in this expression, is customarily used with the price, as you say: "I bought such-and-such for such-and-such." The meaning is: who will take on for me three things, and I will appoint him over the people? Then he explained these three: that he fast by day, stand in prayer by night, and not become angry. A man from the people, whom the eye looked down upon, stood up and said: "I [will]." He repeated to him: "You fast by day, stand [in prayer] by night, and do not become angry?" He said: "Yes." So he dismissed him.

The next day, al-Yasa' sat in his assembly and presented his statement to the people. The same man stood up and said: "I [will]." Al-Yasa' understood that the man had resolve and determination to carry out this task, so he appointed him over the people.

The scholars have discussed these three conditions which Sayyidna al-Yasa', peace be upon him, made the grounds for the appointment (*istikhlaf*, appointing a successor). They said: the one who fasts by day fasts from what God has permitted outside of fasting, and one who fasts from what God has permitted will by greater priority abstain from what God has forbidden, and so by this he guarantees his distance from what is forbidden. The one who stands in prayer by night gives up his rest and his comfort so that he may find intimacy with his Lord, and whoever has this quality does not take the appointment for luxury and ease, but takes it to bear its burdens. Otherwise, if he wanted luxury, he would sleep the night to his heart's content.

As for not becoming angry, it is a quality that must be present in everyone who governs subjects or sits in a judgment seat between people. It is well known that subjects have various dispositions and diverse characters, so whoever takes charge of their affairs must be forbearing and not angry, because anger veils the intellect, so one cannot choose among alternatives, and does not handle governance well.

Therefore they said to the judge when he becomes angry: "Return yourself," meaning: you are not fit for the office of judgeship. So: "and do not become angry," because the intellect is affected by anger, so its judgments differ in ruling, and the faculties of the soul also differ, so the ruling is not valid.

They said regarding the matter of not becoming angry: Satan was unable to interfere with fasting by day and standing [in prayer] by night, so he wished to enter through the side of not becoming angry. He sent his offspring to make him angry, but Dhu al-Kifl, peace be upon him, did not become angry. He said to them: "Lift your hands from him, and I will take care of this matter myself." Dhu al-Kifl used to sleep only one sleep at midday (*qaylulah*, the midday rest), which was all he slept by night and day, and he would order his servant that no one should enter upon him at this time. So Satan would watch for this time, knock on Dhu al-Kifl's door, and create a commotion, saying: "I am a man whom my people have wronged, and they did such-and-such to me, and I want you to give me justice against them."

Dhu al-Kifl said: "Do you not know that this is the time when I rest? Go away and come at a time when I sit to judge between you, and I will rule on your case."

On the next day, Satan came and did as he had done the day before. On the third day he found the door locked, so he entered to Dhu al-Kifl by his own special method. They said: he entered through a window in the house while the guard was negligent, and he knocked on the door of Dhu al-Kifl's chamber. When [Dhu al-Kifl] saw him he said: "How did you enter?" [Satan] was confounded. [Dhu al-Kifl] said: "Then you are he" — that is, Satan. [Satan] said: "By God, we have striven hard to make you angry, but we did not succeed," and then he left him and departed.

As for the scholars' disagreement about the messengership of Dhu al-Kifl, I want to hold the scholars above disagreement on something where we can meet. They said: *al-kafl* comes from *al-takafful* (undertaking responsibility), as in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿and Zakariyya was made her guardian﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37]. And *al-kifl* means the helper.

Those who said he was a messenger based this on two matters. The first: that God mentioned him among the messengers. The second: that al-Yasa', peace be upon him, appointed him as successor, and God, glory be to Him, remained silent about this appointment and did not change it, and this is an affirmation of the appointment and an approval of it, just as God, glory be to Him, approved for Musa, peace be upon him, when he asked his Lord to support him with his brother Harun. He said: ﴿And my brother Harun, he is more eloquent than me in speech, so send him with me as a helper to confirm me...﴾ [al-Qasas: 34].

Others said: rather, he was a man who volunteered for the call. The people in his time had become corrupt, and he saw that this corruption could not be set right except by a man who had integrity in judgment and uprightness in ruling between people. He saw these qualities in himself, so he offered his people that he would take charge of their affairs and govern them with justice, and they agreed to him. So, in the view of these scholars, Dhu al-Kifl was not a messenger, but a man who volunteered with a method like the methods of the messengers.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 38, verses 49–51 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This﴾, i.e., what has preceded of the procession of the messengers, ﴿is a reminder﴾, a reminder, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that if one of them errs, the other may remind her﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].

It means: this which We have mentioned of the procession of the messengers and of the stance of the nations toward them, and how they bore the vileness of their people and the scant courtesy they showed their prophets, and how they endured audacity with the tongue and with the limbs. We mention this to Muhammad, who meets from his people what he meets of harm, so that he may remember that he is not an innovation among the messengers, and that what befell his fellow messengers must also befall him. And if we measure trial by the measure of the message, then Muhammad's share of this harm (ﷺ) is greater than the share of all the messengers.

So His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is a reminder…﴾ [Sad: 49] is a consolation to our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that he knows he is not an innovation in this, and that his greatness lies in receiving the folly of his people. For when a people act foolishly toward the Messenger, this indicates that they profit from the corruption that is widespread among their people, and the Messenger came only to put an end to this corruption. Therefore the Messenger must necessarily be an adversary to these people, and whenever he confronts their corruption, their enmity toward him intensifies, along with their harm, their mockery of him, and their accusing him of lying, sorcery, and madness, and so on.

This, then, is a Sunnah of Allah, Exalted is He, toward everyone who takes up the call and confronts corruption in society: he must find someone who dares against him, accuses him falsely, and tries to bring him down and cast doubt on his intention. This is a natural reaction. When the caller finds it, he should be glad of it, for it is a sign and an indication of his success in his endeavour, and that he has struck them and enraged them.

And His saying, Glory be to Him: ﴿And indeed, for the righteous there is a good return﴾ [Sad: 49], i.e., a good place of return to Allah on the Day of Resurrection. So this speaks of the Hereafter and of the good recompense awaiting him (ﷺ). In the verse there are two gifts to the Messenger of Allah. The first: his consolation (ﷺ) in His saying, ﴿This is a reminder…﴾ [Sad: 49], and then ﴿And indeed, for the righteous there is a good return﴾ [Sad: 49], as if He, Exalted is He, says: this which We have mentioned is a reminder for Muhammad so that We may console him, but more important than that is the good recompense awaiting him in the Hereafter. The conjunction "wa" here links ﴿And indeed, for the righteous there is a good return﴾ [Sad: 49] to ﴿This is a reminder…﴾ [Sad: 49].

As for "the righteous" (al-muttaqun), its root is waqā, meaning to place a barrier between a thing that would harm and oneself; ittaqā al-shay' means to place between oneself and the thing a shield that protects. When we look at this root in the Qur'an, we find that the Exalted One commands taqwa as an obligation that requires a person to shield himself from what would bring him evil. This root has come in the forms: "ittaqū Allah" (fear Allah), "ittaqū Rabbakum" (fear your Lord), "ittaqūnī" (fear Me), "ittaqū al-nār" (fear the Fire), and "ittaqū al-fitnah" (beware of trial).

All of these converge on a single meaning, because Allah, as we have said, has attributes of majesty (jalal) and attributes of beauty (jamal). So the meaning of "ittaqū Allah" is: place between yourselves and the attributes of majesty of Allah a shield, such as the Avenger, the Compelling, the Subduer, and so on.

These attributes are what frighten the opponent and restrain him. So beware the attributes of majesty of Allah, for He is able to seize you, and you have no endurance against the vengeance of Allah or against the effects of these attributes.

In the same sense: "ittaqū al-nār" (beware the Fire), for it is one of the hosts of Allah and an effect of the attributes of majesty.

In one place in the Qur'an taqwa occurs in the form "wa-ittaqū" without mention of that from which one guards, as if this form came to indicate the comprehensiveness of taqwa or taqwa in its absolute sense. So it means: beware Allah, beware the Fire, beware trial, and so on.

The meaning of ﴿a good place of return﴾ [Sad: 49] is: a good return. But which return? The scholars have spoken philosophically about the return, saying: it is the return of the soul to the bodies on the Day of Resurrection. This is words of no weight, because we understand the return and the coming back when we consider the first creation, and the Creator, Exalted is He, before creating the creation took a covenant from them while they were still in the stage of the atoms (dharr).

As He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants and made them testify concerning themselves, [saying], "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we have testified." [This] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were of this unaware," or say, "Only our fathers associated others with Allah before, and we were [merely] descendants after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172–173].

So: the natural faith in the realm of the atoms and the testimony to Allah, Exalted is He, that He is the Lord, the Creator, the Nourisher, requires that the return and the coming back be to Him, for reckoning. Did you meet this testimony with obedience or with disobedience? Whoever fulfilled the old covenant and carried it over into the new covenant has succeeded and has a good return. As for whoever wronged himself and violated the covenant he took upon himself, he has lost and failed, and in the Hereafter he has the return of evil and ill.

Since "a good return" is a general and summary word, the Exalted One wished to detail it and clarify it for us, so He said: ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence whose gates are opened for them﴾ [Sad: 50]. So the phrase "Gardens of Eden" is an apposition (badal) to "a good return." It is as if the Exalted One confined the good return to the Gardens of Eden. The word "jannat" is the plural of "jannah," which is a place full of intertwined trees that conceal one who walks beneath them, or because it covers over (yajunnu) the one who walks in it and holds him back from leaving it or from needing anything else, since in it is everything he needs. This is also the meaning of "garden" in this world, and from it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And present to them the parable of two men: We made for one of them two gardens of grapevines…﴾ [al-Kahf: 32].

Like the garden in which Adam (peace be upon him) dwelt, in which he was to receive from Allah the test of obligation: "do" and "do not do." But some say that Adam was in the Garden of the Hereafter, and Allah expelled him from it to the world. This does not stand, because the first report from Allah about Adam did not say, "I created him for the Garden," but said: ﴿Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].

As for the matter of his entering the Garden, namely the garden of this world, that is because when you wish to train a person in a certain task, you must necessarily provide for him lodging and sustenance, and supply him with the means of his life in the manner that allows him to train and to carry out the mission for which he was charged. Thus Allah did with Adam. When he forgot what Allah had commanded him and followed Satan, his nature changed, and he was no longer fit to dwell in this garden, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So when they tasted of the tree, their private parts became apparent to them…﴾ [al-A'raf: 22].

This was the first time Adam felt shame at his nakedness, because he had contravened the command of his Lord. Likewise, if you see a nakedness appearing on the earth until the Hour is established, know that it is the result of contravening the method of Allah or the suspension of one of His rulings. Otherwise, what made this opening in Adam a nakedness, when it does not differ from any similar opening in the body? What is the difference between it and the opening of the mouth, for example? So then: when did it become nakedness?

It became nakedness when it acquired filth from which human nature recoils. And how did this filth come about? It came about because he ate contrary to the method of his Lord, as proof: when he ate according to what Allah commanded, there were no excretions for him; he would eat from the provision of Allah, eating only to the measure of sustaining life.

But when he disobeyed and ate from the tree, excretions formed and their filthy effect appeared: ﴿and they began to fasten over themselves some leaves of the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 22]; he wanted to cover this nakedness and conceal it. But it became a constant habit of man until eternity: a nakedness that is neither concealed nor averted. So then: it became nakedness through disobedience.

Therefore, we find them in wars and battlefields giving the soldiers nutritious tablets that benefit the body and leave no waste and do not overburden the stomach.

Had Adam paid heed to Satan's whispering, he would not have obeyed him nor eaten from the tree, because he deceived them by saying: ﴿Your Lord has forbidden you this tree only that you become angels or become of the eternal﴾ [al-A'raf: 20], while he himself asks Allah to grant him respite until the day they are resurrected. Had he known that this tree would keep him alive and make him eternal, he would have eaten from it himself. Did he not say: ﴿My Lord, give me respite until the day they are resurrected﴾ [Sad: 79]?

So: Satan was a liar, but Adam did not pay heed to his lie. Exalted is He said: ﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115].

But why did Adam (peace be upon him) fall into this trial? They said: because Adam would be the father of all mankind, and he would represent two categories of them: a category protected from error, namely the prophets and messengers, and a category that errs, namely the common people. So both of these images had to be represented in his life. Disobedience did occur from him while he was in the Garden during the period of the test of obligation, as we have said, and this disobedience does not contradict the infallibility of the prophets, because he had not yet been made a prophet. But Adam repented, and Allah accepted his repentance: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He turned to him in forgiveness…﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37].

And He said: ﴿Then his Lord chose him, and turned to him in forgiveness and guided him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122].

So: the choosing and selection for prophethood came after the ordeal he had fallen into, and after the choosing, Adam was granted the infallibility of the prophets. The phrase ﴿Then his Lord chose him…﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122] indicates sequence (ta'qib) and the existence of an interval between Adam's disobedience and his choosing.

So: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Gardens of Eden…﴾ [Sad: 50] means: in the abode of recompense. And the meaning of "Eden" is: a permanent residence that does not pass away and does not end. He said "Eden" because the gardens of this world benefit their owner for a period and then vanish: either a calamity strikes them, as in His saying concerning the people of the garden: ﴿Indeed, We have tested them as We tested the owners of the garden, when they swore to harvest it at morning, and did not make exception. So there went around it a visitation from your Lord while they were asleep, and it became as though harvested﴾ [al-Qalam: 17–20], or he himself dies and leaves it to another.

Therefore, Allah, Exalted is He, wished to reassure the people of His obedience that the Garden He has prepared for them is lasting and permanent, gardens of enduring, everlasting residence, whose bliss will not escape you nor will you escape it.

His saying, Glory be to Him: ﴿with gates opened for them﴾ [Sad: 50]: "mufattahah" is a passive participle indicating emphasis and the abundance of the opening of the gates. Who opens them? It is permissible that the guardians open them at the moment they see the people of the Garden approaching, welcoming them: ﴿until, when they reach it and its gates are opened, and its keepers say to them, "Peace be upon you; you have done well, so enter it to abide"﴾ [al-Zumar: 73].

As we see, for example, in great hotels, guards and chamberlains stand at the door, and when the visitor arrives they open the door for him. But when this matter has advanced, we have seen doors open by themselves automatically upon approaching them, and if the visitor enters, they close automatically too. So it is permissible that the gates open by the action of the angels, or that they open by the mere will of the people of the Garden: when one wishes to enter, it opens for him without intervention from anyone.

If mankind has reached this level in the matter of opening doors, then this progress confirms what the Qur'an brought. Among this is also His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And were it not that mankind would be one nation, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses and stairways upon which they would ascend﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 33].

We have seen these roofs and these stairways, and by them may be meant the staircases and elevators in which we ascend now. This speech was revealed more than fourteen centuries ago to an unlettered, nomadic people who did not know buildings, but dwelt in tents and houses of hair and wool.

So: the Qur'an contains glimpses that show you that in the Book of Allah there is a store for everything that happens in people's lives. If you marvel at something in the Book of Allah, know that reality confirms it, and that you, O creatures, will reach in your sciences and advancements the like of what you marvel at. If you have been able to do that, then allow Allah to do it all the more.

Then He, Exalted is He, says in describing the people of the Garden: ﴿reclining therein﴾ [Sad: 51]. The reclining (muttaki') is what lies between sleeping and sitting, or between sleeping and sitting upright; for there is a difference between qa'ada and jalasa, though the meaning is one: qa'ada is from standing, one was standing and then sat; jalasa is from lying down, one was lying and then sat up.

When a person is standing, he bears his whole weight on the two feet; if he tires of standing, he sits, and in sitting the weight of the body falls on the buttocks; if he tires of sitting, he reclines on his side. This is a posture between sitting and lying on the ground, in which the weight of the body is distributed, and it is more restful for the person.

Therefore Allah chose it for the people of the Garden, and the wife of the Aziz chose it for the women she hosted. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And she prepared for them a reclining couch﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. So the "muttaka" indicates that the sitting does not tire, and that reclining is the posture in which a person takes his rest.

And He, Exalted is He, said concerning the people of the Garden: ﴿reclining upon furnishings whose linings are of brocade, and the fruit of the two gardens will be within reach﴾ [al-Rahman: 54].

And He also said in Surat al-Rahman: ﴿reclining on green cushions and beautiful Abqari carpets﴾ [al-Rahman: 76].

And He also said in showing the reclining place of the people of the Garden: ﴿reclining therein upon couches﴾ [al-Kahf: 31].

So: the people of the Garden recline either on furnishings lined with brocade, which is thick, coarse silk, resembling what we now call satin (al-sattan). If these furnishings have brocade as their filling and lining, what then of their outer surface?

The word "rafraf" means what we now call the cornices found, for example, on curtains. "Al-arā'ik" is the plural of arika, which is a bed on which ornaments and curtains are placed, something like a canopy bed, for example. These are the reclining places of the people of the Garden.

But what comes after reclining? For the completeness of bliss, food and drink are necessary, for one does not recline and fast. Rather: ﴿they will call therein for abundant fruit and drink﴾ [Sad: 51]. So the greeting presented to them is what their souls desire. That is: nothing is offered to them against their wish; rather, according to what they desire and what they crave. The greeting is not binding on all, since it may not coincide with a desire in the soul. He presented fruit although it is luxury and enjoyment after the natural and necessary sustenance. They said: the existence of fruit or enjoyment of fruit is evidence of the existence of necessities a fortiori.

His saying ﴿and drink﴾ [Sad: 51] means the drink extracted from grapes. He singled out fruit and drink because they did not exist in the environment in which the Qur'an was revealed, so they had a delight for them; for they knew in their food only dates, wheat, and barley. So He mentioned to them what they desire of food and drink.

In another place He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And fruit of what they choose, and the flesh of birds of what they desire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 20–21].

In Surah al-Baqarah, He shows them that the fruit of the Hereafter differs from the fruit of this world they know, even though the two resemble each other. The shape and color are the same, but the taste is different. Allah says: ﴿Whenever they are provided with a provision of its fruit, they say, "This is what we were provided with before," and they are given it in semblance; and for them therein are purified spouses, and they abide therein eternally﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25].

So: the fruit is (in name and appearance) the fruit, an apple like an apple, to the point that you say, "This is what I ate in the world," while in reality it is entirely different, because it is prepared for you by the perfection of power.

In other passages the Noble Qur'an describes the gathering of the people of Paradise. It speaks once of the couches and reclining places, saying: ﴿Therein are raised couches, and cups set in place, and cushions arranged, and carpets spread out﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 13-16].

Al-namariq is the plural of namraqah, which is the cushion upon which one reclines. Al-zarabi is the plural of zaribah, which is the embroidered carpet. When He speaks of drinking vessels, He says once "akwab" (cups), once "abariq" (ewers), and once "ka's" (goblet).

All of these are containers for drink, but there is a difference between these three. The kub (cup) is the vessel that has no handle or spout; a handle means a grip by which it is held, and the spout is what we call the "bazbuz," from which water is poured. If it has a handle or a spout, it is called ibriq (ewer). If there is drink in the kub, it is called ka's (goblet); that is, the ka's is the kub when it is full, and when it is empty it is a kub.

Among the customs of the Arabs regarding cups: one of them does not drink all that is in it, but leaves a quantity of drink in it and then pours it out on the ground. This indicates the absence of greed and avarice, or indicates the fullness of the eye and self-sufficiency.

The poet expressed this meaning by his saying:
And from the cup of the generous, a share is for the earth

When we were invited to the food of one of the brothers, before going to it we would eat a light meal, or a dish we call "tabaq al-karamah" (the dish of dignity), so that we would not sit to the food while eager for it, for it is not becoming of the generous to approach food greedily, as if he had never seen food before.

Also among the customs of the Arabs in their drinking is that they do not fill the cup to its brim, so that the drinker can distinguish the drink from the cup in which it was placed, and this indicates the clarity of the drink or the clarity of the cup.

Therefore their poet said:
Were it not for the cup being half-filled, we would think it
In the hand of its cupbearer standing by itself

That is: were the cup filled, you would think it was a cup without drink, or drink without a cup.

But what do the people of Paradise seek after reclining, after eating and drinking of what their souls desire? They say: after these blessings are complete, a person longs for a beautiful companion whom he desires to be his alone, with no one else sharing her. Therefore Allah says after this: ﴿And with them are those restraining their gaze...﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 38, verses 49–51 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This﴾, i.e., what has preceded of the procession of the messengers, ﴿is a reminder﴾, a reminder, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that if one of them errs, the other may remind her﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].

It means: this which We have mentioned of the procession of the messengers and of the stance of the nations toward them, and how they bore the vileness of their people and the scant courtesy they showed their prophets, and how they endured audacity with the tongue and with the limbs. We mention this to Muhammad, who meets from his people what he meets of harm, so that he may remember that he is not an innovation among the messengers, and that what befell his fellow messengers must also befall him. And if we measure trial by the measure of the message, then Muhammad's share of this harm (ﷺ) is greater than the share of all the messengers.

So His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is a reminder…﴾ [Sad: 49] is a consolation to our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that he knows he is not an innovation in this, and that his greatness lies in receiving the folly of his people. For when a people act foolishly toward the Messenger, this indicates that they profit from the corruption that is widespread among their people, and the Messenger came only to put an end to this corruption. Therefore the Messenger must necessarily be an adversary to these people, and whenever he confronts their corruption, their enmity toward him intensifies, along with their harm, their mockery of him, and their accusing him of lying, sorcery, and madness, and so on.

This, then, is a Sunnah of Allah, Exalted is He, toward everyone who takes up the call and confronts corruption in society: he must find someone who dares against him, accuses him falsely, and tries to bring him down and cast doubt on his intention. This is a natural reaction. When the caller finds it, he should be glad of it, for it is a sign and an indication of his success in his endeavour, and that he has struck them and enraged them.

And His saying, Glory be to Him: ﴿And indeed, for the righteous there is a good return﴾ [Sad: 49], i.e., a good place of return to Allah on the Day of Resurrection. So this speaks of the Hereafter and of the good recompense awaiting him (ﷺ). In the verse there are two gifts to the Messenger of Allah. The first: his consolation (ﷺ) in His saying, ﴿This is a reminder…﴾ [Sad: 49], and then ﴿And indeed, for the righteous there is a good return﴾ [Sad: 49], as if He, Exalted is He, says: this which We have mentioned is a reminder for Muhammad so that We may console him, but more important than that is the good recompense awaiting him in the Hereafter. The conjunction "wa" here links ﴿And indeed, for the righteous there is a good return﴾ [Sad: 49] to ﴿This is a reminder…﴾ [Sad: 49].

As for "the righteous" (al-muttaqun), its root is waqā, meaning to place a barrier between a thing that would harm and oneself; ittaqā al-shay' means to place between oneself and the thing a shield that protects. When we look at this root in the Qur'an, we find that the Exalted One commands taqwa as an obligation that requires a person to shield himself from what would bring him evil. This root has come in the forms: "ittaqū Allah" (fear Allah), "ittaqū Rabbakum" (fear your Lord), "ittaqūnī" (fear Me), "ittaqū al-nār" (fear the Fire), and "ittaqū al-fitnah" (beware of trial).

All of these converge on a single meaning, because Allah, as we have said, has attributes of majesty (jalal) and attributes of beauty (jamal). So the meaning of "ittaqū Allah" is: place between yourselves and the attributes of majesty of Allah a shield, such as the Avenger, the Compelling, the Subduer, and so on.

These attributes are what frighten the opponent and restrain him. So beware the attributes of majesty of Allah, for He is able to seize you, and you have no endurance against the vengeance of Allah or against the effects of these attributes.

In the same sense: "ittaqū al-nār" (beware the Fire), for it is one of the hosts of Allah and an effect of the attributes of majesty.

In one place in the Qur'an taqwa occurs in the form "wa-ittaqū" without mention of that from which one guards, as if this form came to indicate the comprehensiveness of taqwa or taqwa in its absolute sense. So it means: beware Allah, beware the Fire, beware trial, and so on.

The meaning of ﴿a good place of return﴾ [Sad: 49] is: a good return. But which return? The scholars have spoken philosophically about the return, saying: it is the return of the soul to the bodies on the Day of Resurrection. This is words of no weight, because we understand the return and the coming back when we consider the first creation, and the Creator, Exalted is He, before creating the creation took a covenant from them while they were still in the stage of the atoms (dharr).
