Therefore Allah chose it for the people of the Garden, and the wife of the Aziz chose it for the women she hosted. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And she prepared for them a reclining couch﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. So the "muttaka" indicates that the sitting does not tire, and that reclining is the posture in which a person takes his rest.

And He, Exalted is He, said concerning the people of the Garden: ﴿reclining upon furnishings whose linings are of brocade, and the fruit of the two gardens will be within reach﴾ [al-Rahman: 54].

And He also said in Surat al-Rahman: ﴿reclining on green cushions and beautiful Abqari carpets﴾ [al-Rahman: 76].

And He also said in showing the reclining place of the people of the Garden: ﴿reclining therein upon couches﴾ [al-Kahf: 31].

So: the people of the Garden recline either on furnishings lined with brocade, which is thick, coarse silk, resembling what we now call satin (al-sattan). If these furnishings have brocade as their filling and lining, what then of their outer surface?

The word "rafraf" means what we now call the cornices found, for example, on curtains. "Al-arā'ik" is the plural of arika, which is a bed on which ornaments and curtains are placed, something like a canopy bed, for example. These are the reclining places of the people of the Garden.

But what comes after reclining? For the completeness of bliss, food and drink are necessary, for one does not recline and fast. Rather: ﴿they will call therein for abundant fruit and drink﴾ [Sad: 51]. So the greeting presented to them is what their souls desire. That is: nothing is offered to them against their wish; rather, according to what they desire and what they crave. The greeting is not binding on all, since it may not coincide with a desire in the soul. He presented fruit although it is luxury and enjoyment after the natural and necessary sustenance. They said: the existence of fruit or enjoyment of fruit is evidence of the existence of necessities a fortiori.

His saying ﴿and drink﴾ [Sad: 51] means the drink extracted from grapes. He singled out fruit and drink because they did not exist in the environment in which the Qur'an was revealed, so they had a delight for them; for they knew in their food only dates, wheat, and barley. So He mentioned to them what they desire of food and drink.

In another place He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And fruit of what they choose, and the flesh of birds of what they desire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 20–21].

In Surah al-Baqarah, He shows them that the fruit of the Hereafter differs from the fruit of this world they know, even though the two resemble each other. The shape and color are the same, but the taste is different. Allah says: ﴿Whenever they are provided with a provision of its fruit, they say, "This is what we were provided with before," and they are given it in semblance; and for them therein are purified spouses, and they abide therein eternally﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25].

So: the fruit is (in name and appearance) the fruit, an apple like an apple, to the point that you say, "This is what I ate in the world," while in reality it is entirely different, because it is prepared for you by the perfection of power.

In other passages the Noble Qur'an describes the gathering of the people of Paradise. It speaks once of the couches and reclining places, saying: ﴿Therein are raised couches, and cups set in place, and cushions arranged, and carpets spread out﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 13-16].

Al-namariq is the plural of namraqah, which is the cushion upon which one reclines. Al-zarabi is the plural of zaribah, which is the embroidered carpet. When He speaks of drinking vessels, He says once "akwab" (cups), once "abariq" (ewers), and once "ka's" (goblet).

All of these are containers for drink, but there is a difference between these three. The kub (cup) is the vessel that has no handle or spout; a handle means a grip by which it is held, and the spout is what we call the "bazbuz," from which water is poured. If it has a handle or a spout, it is called ibriq (ewer). If there is drink in the kub, it is called ka's (goblet); that is, the ka's is the kub when it is full, and when it is empty it is a kub.

Among the customs of the Arabs regarding cups: one of them does not drink all that is in it, but leaves a quantity of drink in it and then pours it out on the ground. This indicates the absence of greed and avarice, or indicates the fullness of the eye and self-sufficiency.

The poet expressed this meaning by his saying:
And from the cup of the generous, a share is for the earth

When we were invited to the food of one of the brothers, before going to it we would eat a light meal, or a dish we call "tabaq al-karamah" (the dish of dignity), so that we would not sit to the food while eager for it, for it is not becoming of the generous to approach food greedily, as if he had never seen food before.

Also among the customs of the Arabs in their drinking is that they do not fill the cup to its brim, so that the drinker can distinguish the drink from the cup in which it was placed, and this indicates the clarity of the drink or the clarity of the cup.

Therefore their poet said:
Were it not for the cup being half-filled, we would think it
In the hand of its cupbearer standing by itself

That is: were the cup filled, you would think it was a cup without drink, or drink without a cup.

But what do the people of Paradise seek after reclining, after eating and drinking of what their souls desire? They say: after these blessings are complete, a person longs for a beautiful companion whom he desires to be his alone, with no one else sharing her. Therefore Allah says after this: ﴿And with them are those restraining their gaze...﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 38, verses 49–51 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This﴾, i.e., what has preceded of the procession of the messengers, ﴿is a reminder﴾, a reminder, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that if one of them errs, the other may remind her﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].

It means: this which We have mentioned of the procession of the messengers and of the stance of the nations toward them, and how they bore the vileness of their people and the scant courtesy they showed their prophets, and how they endured audacity with the tongue and with the limbs. We mention this to Muhammad, who meets from his people what he meets of harm, so that he may remember that he is not an innovation among the messengers, and that what befell his fellow messengers must also befall him. And if we measure trial by the measure of the message, then Muhammad's share of this harm (ﷺ) is greater than the share of all the messengers.

So His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is a reminder…﴾ [Sad: 49] is a consolation to our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that he knows he is not an innovation in this, and that his greatness lies in receiving the folly of his people. For when a people act foolishly toward the Messenger, this indicates that they profit from the corruption that is widespread among their people, and the Messenger came only to put an end to this corruption. Therefore the Messenger must necessarily be an adversary to these people, and whenever he confronts their corruption, their enmity toward him intensifies, along with their harm, their mockery of him, and their accusing him of lying, sorcery, and madness, and so on.

This, then, is a Sunnah of Allah, Exalted is He, toward everyone who takes up the call and confronts corruption in society: he must find someone who dares against him, accuses him falsely, and tries to bring him down and cast doubt on his intention. This is a natural reaction. When the caller finds it, he should be glad of it, for it is a sign and an indication of his success in his endeavour, and that he has struck them and enraged them.

And His saying, Glory be to Him: ﴿And indeed, for the righteous there is a good return﴾ [Sad: 49], i.e., a good place of return to Allah on the Day of Resurrection. So this speaks of the Hereafter and of the good recompense awaiting him (ﷺ). In the verse there are two gifts to the Messenger of Allah. The first: his consolation (ﷺ) in His saying, ﴿This is a reminder…﴾ [Sad: 49], and then ﴿And indeed, for the righteous there is a good return﴾ [Sad: 49], as if He, Exalted is He, says: this which We have mentioned is a reminder for Muhammad so that We may console him, but more important than that is the good recompense awaiting him in the Hereafter. The conjunction "wa" here links ﴿And indeed, for the righteous there is a good return﴾ [Sad: 49] to ﴿This is a reminder…﴾ [Sad: 49].

As for "the righteous" (al-muttaqun), its root is waqā, meaning to place a barrier between a thing that would harm and oneself; ittaqā al-shay' means to place between oneself and the thing a shield that protects. When we look at this root in the Qur'an, we find that the Exalted One commands taqwa as an obligation that requires a person to shield himself from what would bring him evil. This root has come in the forms: "ittaqū Allah" (fear Allah), "ittaqū Rabbakum" (fear your Lord), "ittaqūnī" (fear Me), "ittaqū al-nār" (fear the Fire), and "ittaqū al-fitnah" (beware of trial).

All of these converge on a single meaning, because Allah, as we have said, has attributes of majesty (jalal) and attributes of beauty (jamal). So the meaning of "ittaqū Allah" is: place between yourselves and the attributes of majesty of Allah a shield, such as the Avenger, the Compelling, the Subduer, and so on.

These attributes are what frighten the opponent and restrain him. So beware the attributes of majesty of Allah, for He is able to seize you, and you have no endurance against the vengeance of Allah or against the effects of these attributes.

In the same sense: "ittaqū al-nār" (beware the Fire), for it is one of the hosts of Allah and an effect of the attributes of majesty.

In one place in the Qur'an taqwa occurs in the form "wa-ittaqū" without mention of that from which one guards, as if this form came to indicate the comprehensiveness of taqwa or taqwa in its absolute sense. So it means: beware Allah, beware the Fire, beware trial, and so on.

The meaning of ﴿a good place of return﴾ [Sad: 49] is: a good return. But which return? The scholars have spoken philosophically about the return, saying: it is the return of the soul to the bodies on the Day of Resurrection. This is words of no weight, because we understand the return and the coming back when we consider the first creation, and the Creator, Exalted is He, before creating the creation took a covenant from them while they were still in the stage of the atoms (dharr).

As He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants and made them testify concerning themselves, [saying], "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we have testified." [This] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were of this unaware," or say, "Only our fathers associated others with Allah before, and we were [merely] descendants after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172–173].

So: the natural faith in the realm of the atoms and the testimony to Allah, Exalted is He, that He is the Lord, the Creator, the Nourisher, requires that the return and the coming back be to Him, for reckoning. Did you meet this testimony with obedience or with disobedience? Whoever fulfilled the old covenant and carried it over into the new covenant has succeeded and has a good return. As for whoever wronged himself and violated the covenant he took upon himself, he has lost and failed, and in the Hereafter he has the return of evil and ill.

Since "a good return" is a general and summary word, the Exalted One wished to detail it and clarify it for us, so He said: ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence whose gates are opened for them﴾ [Sad: 50]. So the phrase "Gardens of Eden" is an apposition (badal) to "a good return." It is as if the Exalted One confined the good return to the Gardens of Eden. The word "jannat" is the plural of "jannah," which is a place full of intertwined trees that conceal one who walks beneath them, or because it covers over (yajunnu) the one who walks in it and holds him back from leaving it or from needing anything else, since in it is everything he needs. This is also the meaning of "garden" in this world, and from it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And present to them the parable of two men: We made for one of them two gardens of grapevines…﴾ [al-Kahf: 32].

Like the garden in which Adam (peace be upon him) dwelt, in which he was to receive from Allah the test of obligation: "do" and "do not do." But some say that Adam was in the Garden of the Hereafter, and Allah expelled him from it to the world. This does not stand, because the first report from Allah about Adam did not say, "I created him for the Garden," but said: ﴿Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].

As for the matter of his entering the Garden, namely the garden of this world, that is because when you wish to train a person in a certain task, you must necessarily provide for him lodging and sustenance, and supply him with the means of his life in the manner that allows him to train and to carry out the mission for which he was charged. Thus Allah did with Adam. When he forgot what Allah had commanded him and followed Satan, his nature changed, and he was no longer fit to dwell in this garden, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So when they tasted of the tree, their private parts became apparent to them…﴾ [al-A'raf: 22].

This was the first time Adam felt shame at his nakedness, because he had contravened the command of his Lord. Likewise, if you see a nakedness appearing on the earth until the Hour is established, know that it is the result of contravening the method of Allah or the suspension of one of His rulings. Otherwise, what made this opening in Adam a nakedness, when it does not differ from any similar opening in the body? What is the difference between it and the opening of the mouth, for example? So then: when did it become nakedness?

It became nakedness when it acquired filth from which human nature recoils. And how did this filth come about? It came about because he ate contrary to the method of his Lord, as proof: when he ate according to what Allah commanded, there were no excretions for him; he would eat from the provision of Allah, eating only to the measure of sustaining life.

But when he disobeyed and ate from the tree, excretions formed and their filthy effect appeared: ﴿and they began to fasten over themselves some leaves of the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 22]; he wanted to cover this nakedness and conceal it. But it became a constant habit of man until eternity: a nakedness that is neither concealed nor averted. So then: it became nakedness through disobedience.

Therefore, we find them in wars and battlefields giving the soldiers nutritious tablets that benefit the body and leave no waste and do not overburden the stomach.

Had Adam paid heed to Satan's whispering, he would not have obeyed him nor eaten from the tree, because he deceived them by saying: ﴿Your Lord has forbidden you this tree only that you become angels or become of the eternal﴾ [al-A'raf: 20], while he himself asks Allah to grant him respite until the day they are resurrected. Had he known that this tree would keep him alive and make him eternal, he would have eaten from it himself. Did he not say: ﴿My Lord, give me respite until the day they are resurrected﴾ [Sad: 79]?

So: Satan was a liar, but Adam did not pay heed to his lie. Exalted is He said: ﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115].

But why did Adam (peace be upon him) fall into this trial? They said: because Adam would be the father of all mankind, and he would represent two categories of them: a category protected from error, namely the prophets and messengers, and a category that errs, namely the common people. So both of these images had to be represented in his life. Disobedience did occur from him while he was in the Garden during the period of the test of obligation, as we have said, and this disobedience does not contradict the infallibility of the prophets, because he had not yet been made a prophet. But Adam repented, and Allah accepted his repentance: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He turned to him in forgiveness…﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37].

And He said: ﴿Then his Lord chose him, and turned to him in forgiveness and guided him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122].

So: the choosing and selection for prophethood came after the ordeal he had fallen into, and after the choosing, Adam was granted the infallibility of the prophets. The phrase ﴿Then his Lord chose him…﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122] indicates sequence (ta'qib) and the existence of an interval between Adam's disobedience and his choosing.

So: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Gardens of Eden…﴾ [Sad: 50] means: in the abode of recompense. And the meaning of "Eden" is: a permanent residence that does not pass away and does not end. He said "Eden" because the gardens of this world benefit their owner for a period and then vanish: either a calamity strikes them, as in His saying concerning the people of the garden: ﴿Indeed, We have tested them as We tested the owners of the garden, when they swore to harvest it at morning, and did not make exception. So there went around it a visitation from your Lord while they were asleep, and it became as though harvested﴾ [al-Qalam: 17–20], or he himself dies and leaves it to another.

Therefore, Allah, Exalted is He, wished to reassure the people of His obedience that the Garden He has prepared for them is lasting and permanent, gardens of enduring, everlasting residence, whose bliss will not escape you nor will you escape it.

His saying, Glory be to Him: ﴿with gates opened for them﴾ [Sad: 50]: "mufattahah" is a passive participle indicating emphasis and the abundance of the opening of the gates. Who opens them? It is permissible that the guardians open them at the moment they see the people of the Garden approaching, welcoming them: ﴿until, when they reach it and its gates are opened, and its keepers say to them, "Peace be upon you; you have done well, so enter it to abide"﴾ [al-Zumar: 73].

As we see, for example, in great hotels, guards and chamberlains stand at the door, and when the visitor arrives they open the door for him. But when this matter has advanced, we have seen doors open by themselves automatically upon approaching them, and if the visitor enters, they close automatically too. So it is permissible that the gates open by the action of the angels, or that they open by the mere will of the people of the Garden: when one wishes to enter, it opens for him without intervention from anyone.

If mankind has reached this level in the matter of opening doors, then this progress confirms what the Qur'an brought. Among this is also His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And were it not that mankind would be one nation, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses and stairways upon which they would ascend﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 33].

We have seen these roofs and these stairways, and by them may be meant the staircases and elevators in which we ascend now. This speech was revealed more than fourteen centuries ago to an unlettered, nomadic people who did not know buildings, but dwelt in tents and houses of hair and wool.

So: the Qur'an contains glimpses that show you that in the Book of Allah there is a store for everything that happens in people's lives. If you marvel at something in the Book of Allah, know that reality confirms it, and that you, O creatures, will reach in your sciences and advancements the like of what you marvel at. If you have been able to do that, then allow Allah to do it all the more.

Then He, Exalted is He, says in describing the people of the Garden: ﴿reclining therein﴾ [Sad: 51]. The reclining (muttaki') is what lies between sleeping and sitting, or between sleeping and sitting upright; for there is a difference between qa'ada and jalasa, though the meaning is one: qa'ada is from standing, one was standing and then sat; jalasa is from lying down, one was lying and then sat up.

When a person is standing, he bears his whole weight on the two feet; if he tires of standing, he sits, and in sitting the weight of the body falls on the buttocks; if he tires of sitting, he reclines on his side. This is a posture between sitting and lying on the ground, in which the weight of the body is distributed, and it is more restful for the person.

Therefore Allah chose it for the people of the Garden, and the wife of the Aziz chose it for the women she hosted. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And she prepared for them a reclining couch﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. So the "muttaka" indicates that the sitting does not tire, and that reclining is the posture in which a person takes his rest.

And He, Exalted is He, said concerning the people of the Garden: ﴿reclining upon furnishings whose linings are of brocade, and the fruit of the two gardens will be within reach﴾ [al-Rahman: 54].

And He also said in Surat al-Rahman: ﴿reclining on green cushions and beautiful Abqari carpets﴾ [al-Rahman: 76].

And He also said in showing the reclining place of the people of the Garden: ﴿reclining therein upon couches﴾ [al-Kahf: 31].

So: the people of the Garden recline either on furnishings lined with brocade, which is thick, coarse silk, resembling what we now call satin (al-sattan). If these furnishings have brocade as their filling and lining, what then of their outer surface?

The word "rafraf" means what we now call the cornices found, for example, on curtains. "Al-arā'ik" is the plural of arika, which is a bed on which ornaments and curtains are placed, something like a canopy bed, for example. These are the reclining places of the people of the Garden.

But what comes after reclining? For the completeness of bliss, food and drink are necessary, for one does not recline and fast. Rather: ﴿they will call therein for abundant fruit and drink﴾ [Sad: 51]. So the greeting presented to them is what their souls desire. That is: nothing is offered to them against their wish; rather, according to what they desire and what they crave. The greeting is not binding on all, since it may not coincide with a desire in the soul. He presented fruit although it is luxury and enjoyment after the natural and necessary sustenance. They said: the existence of fruit or enjoyment of fruit is evidence of the existence of necessities a fortiori.

His saying ﴿and drink﴾ [Sad: 51] means the drink extracted from grapes. He singled out fruit and drink because they did not exist in the environment in which the Qur'an was revealed, so they had a delight for them; for they knew in their food only dates, wheat, and barley. So He mentioned to them what they desire of food and drink.

In another place He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And fruit of what they choose, and the flesh of birds of what they desire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 20–21].

In Surah al-Baqarah, He shows them that the fruit of the Hereafter differs from the fruit of this world they know, even though the two resemble each other. The shape and color are the same, but the taste is different. Allah says: ﴿Whenever they are provided with a provision of its fruit, they say, "This is what we were provided with before," and they are given it in semblance; and for them therein are purified spouses, and they abide therein eternally﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25].

So: the fruit is (in name and appearance) the fruit, an apple like an apple, to the point that you say, "This is what I ate in the world," while in reality it is entirely different, because it is prepared for you by the perfection of power.

In other passages the Noble Qur'an describes the gathering of the people of Paradise. It speaks once of the couches and reclining places, saying: ﴿Therein are raised couches, and cups set in place, and cushions arranged, and carpets spread out﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 13-16].

Al-namariq is the plural of namraqah, which is the cushion upon which one reclines. Al-zarabi is the plural of zaribah, which is the embroidered carpet. When He speaks of drinking vessels, He says once "akwab" (cups), once "abariq" (ewers), and once "ka's" (goblet).

All of these are containers for drink, but there is a difference between these three. The kub (cup) is the vessel that has no handle or spout; a handle means a grip by which it is held, and the spout is what we call the "bazbuz," from which water is poured. If it has a handle or a spout, it is called ibriq (ewer). If there is drink in the kub, it is called ka's (goblet); that is, the ka's is the kub when it is full, and when it is empty it is a kub.

Among the customs of the Arabs regarding cups: one of them does not drink all that is in it, but leaves a quantity of drink in it and then pours it out on the ground. This indicates the absence of greed and avarice, or indicates the fullness of the eye and self-sufficiency.

The poet expressed this meaning by his saying:
And from the cup of the generous, a share is for the earth

When we were invited to the food of one of the brothers, before going to it we would eat a light meal, or a dish we call "tabaq al-karamah" (the dish of dignity), so that we would not sit to the food while eager for it, for it is not becoming of the generous to approach food greedily, as if he had never seen food before.

Also among the customs of the Arabs in their drinking is that they do not fill the cup to its brim, so that the drinker can distinguish the drink from the cup in which it was placed, and this indicates the clarity of the drink or the clarity of the cup.

Therefore their poet said:
Were it not for the cup being half-filled, we would think it
In the hand of its cupbearer standing by itself

That is: were the cup filled, you would think it was a cup without drink, or drink without a cup.

But what do the people of Paradise seek after reclining, after eating and drinking of what their souls desire? They say: after these blessings are complete, a person longs for a beautiful companion whom he desires to be his alone, with no one else sharing her. Therefore Allah says after this: ﴿And with them are those restraining their gaze...﴾.

The meaning of ﴿restraining their gaze﴾ [Sad: 52] is that each one of them restrains her eyes so that they do not reach beyond her husband, so no one can hope to look at her. The glance, or the eye, has an effect, and it has speech and a language. An example is the words of God, may He be exalted, in the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿When they saw him, they were struck with awe of him and cut their hands, and they said, "Perfect is God! This is not a man. This is none other than a noble angel."﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. Then He, glorified is He, says, relating what Yusuf said: ﴿He said, "My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to. And unless You turn their plot away from me, I might incline toward them and be among the ignorant."﴾ [Yusuf: 33].

The story concerned one woman, the wife of the al-Aziz (the minister). So how does He say here ﴿what they invite me to...﴾ [Yusuf: 33], and ﴿their plot...﴾ [Yusuf: 33], and ﴿incline toward them...﴾ [Yusuf: 33], in the plural form?

Therefore, it must be that at the moment they saw him, each of them looked at him with a glance from which he deduced that she desired him. So the glance is a language that carries speech and expresses what is in the heart of its owner. For this reason Yusuf spoke of all of them, not of the wife of al-Aziz alone. This is also why, when the king wanted to summon him, he said: ﴿What is the matter with the women who cut their hands...?﴾ [Yusuf: 50], although the matter had begun with the wife of al-Aziz.

Among the glances that carried meanings in our Arabic literature is what is related of Abu Dulama. When he entered upon the caliph, with the notables around him, the caliph wanted to joke with Abu Dulama and said to him: "O Abu Dulama, you will satirize one of us, or I will certainly kill you!" Abu Dulama stood thinking about what to say, and those present began to look at him, each one saying to him with a glance: "Do not satirize me, and you will have whatever gifts you wish." One would encourage him with desire, and another would frighten him with threat.

Finally, Abu Dulama decided to please the caliph and to satirize himself, in hope of the gifts he expected from these notables. Everyone was surprised when Abu Dulama said:

"Let it be known to you, Abu Dulama,
that he is not of the noble nor of nobility.
When he wears the turban, he is a monkey and a pig;
when he takes off the turban, he is..."

Abu Dulama became rich because of this jest.

So the meaning of ﴿restraining their gaze, of equal age﴾ [Sad: 52] is that they lower their gaze away from anyone other than their owner. This is the particular quality sought in a woman specifically, because you find a man, however generous and bountiful he may be, giving everything he owns to whomever he loves, except his wife; he cannot bear for anyone else even to look at her. This is a quality of the believer in this world, and it is also his quality in the Hereafter.

Therefore we say: among the wonders that faith does to its people and among its virtues is that it does not only remove beliefs from hearts or choice from minds, but it also removes inclination from emotion. We have seen this in the story of the Emigrants and the Helpers. Faith removed disbelief from their hearts and removed from their minds love of obstinacy in choosing; then it removed the strongest emotion, the man's emotion toward his wife.

Did not the Helper say to his emigrant brother, who came without his family: "Look at my wives; whichever of them pleases you, I will divorce her so that you may marry her"? To this degree faith acted upon the early believers.

The meaning of ﴿of equal age﴾ [Sad: 52] is that they are equal in beauty or in age, so that no one of them can be distinguished from another. All of them are beautiful of one age, one beauty and one stature. Why? They said: so that eyes remain confined to what one possesses, no one hopes for the others, no one looks, and no eye strays toward what is not its own. If all women were on one level, then why would there be any looking?

Or ﴿of equal age﴾ [Sad: 52] means: like him and suitable for him, changing for him into the form he loves.

As for His saying, ﴿This...﴾ [Sad: 53], it means: what We have mentioned of the Garden and its bliss. All of this that is mentioned is ﴿what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning﴾ [Sad: 53]. But promised by whom? When he entered upon the caliph, with the notables around him, the caliph wanted to joke with Abu Dulama and said to him: "O Abu Dulama, you will satirize one of us, or I will certainly kill you!" Abu Dulama stood thinking about what to say, and those present began to look at him, each one saying to him with a glance: "Do not satirize me, and you will have whatever gifts you wish." One would encourage him with desire, and another would frighten him with threat.

Finally, Abu Dulama decided to please the caliph and to satirize himself, in hope of the gifts he expected from these notables. Everyone was surprised when Abu Dulama said:

"Let it be known to you, Abu Dulama,
that he is not of the noble nor of nobility.
When he wears the turban, he is a monkey and a pig;
when he takes off the turban, he is..."

Abu Dulama became rich because of this jest.

Therefore we say: among the wonders that faith does to its people and among its virtues is that it does not only remove beliefs from hearts or choice from minds, but it also removes inclination from emotion. Al-mahd (the cradle, a bed prepared for resting) is the bedding of a infant that is spread out for it to sleep in comfortably. But the infant has no part in preparing it; his guardian, who takes charge of his affairs, prepares it for him. Likewise, these transgressors have no part in the bed in which they will be cast.

Thus, the use of "mahd" here is in the manner of mockery and derision directed at them. ﴿This, so let them taste it: scalding water and dark, dense pus﴾ [Sad 38:57], meaning let them taste the punishment. Hamim is the hot thing whose heat has become extreme, and ghassaq is the pus of the people of the Fire that flows from them in Hell, and we seek refuge in Allah. You say: "his eye ghasaqat," meaning its tears flowed.

Otherwise, where is al-muhl (molten dregs), and where is the tree of zaqqum, whose fruit is like the heads of devils, and the other kinds of punishment that Allah prepared for these transgressors?

After Allah, glorified is He, gave us this clarifying comparison between the reward of the good, God-conscious people and the destiny of the wicked transgressors, He, glorified is He, wished to distinguish between the companionship of the good and the companionship of the wicked. The companionship of the good helps you in obedience and helps you toward goodness, while the companionship of the wicked drags you toward evil and calls you to disobedience.

For example, in schools, how many a student has excelled because he walked alongside a companion of goodness who helped him with his lessons, urged him to study, and warned him of the bad outcome at the end of the year if he neglected his work. And on the other hand, how many a student has failed because he accompanied wicked companions who enticed him to skip classes, took him to the street, and to improper conduct.

In the end, the successful student must thank the companion who took his hand toward goodness, and the failing student must blame the companion who enticed him, misled him, and wasted his opportunity.

This passage depicts one of the scenes of the Day of Resurrection, in which the people of evil, who cooperated in it and gathered for its sake, speak to one another: the intimate friends in wickedness. This dialogue has three parties: the angels, the guardians of the Fire; the leaders of disbelief who went ahead into the Fire; and then their followers, those whom they led astray. The angels say to the leaders of disbelief: ﴿This is a host rushing in with you﴾ [Sad: 59], alerting the people of the Fire that a group of their followers is coming to them.

The meaning of ﴿muqtahim﴾ [Sad: 59] is: entering the Fire forcefully and quickly. But how does the one who enters hasten, when he is entering the Fire? They said: because he does not walk by his own will; rather, he is compelled to be present and pushed into entering against his wish, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿On the Day they will be pushed toward the Fire of Hell, with a vehement push﴾ [al-Tur: 13].

Al-fawj (the host) is the group or company, as we say: the company of pilgrims, or the company of travelers.

So what did the leaders of disbelief who are in the Fire say? They said: ﴿No welcome for them! Indeed, they will burn in the Fire﴾ [Sad: 59]. That is: no spaciousness, no greeting, no honor. Such is the condition of friends in evil: in the Hereafter this intimacy and friendship turn into enmity, and each one curses his companion. The leader curses the follower, and the follower curses the leader. Here are the leaders saying to their followers: ﴿No welcome for them...﴾ [Sad: 59]. And why should we welcome them? Did they come to rescue us from what we are in? Or even to lighten it for us? No, they came to the Fire and to be scorched by its heat.

"So you will not find any change in the way of Allah" (Fatir 35:43).

For example, at Badr we defeated them, killed some of them and took captives, and not a single year passed before Uhud came. In it the disbelievers marched from Makkah to near Madinah, and the indications pointed to the victory of the Muslims, but they opposed the method of God by not obeying the command of their Messenger.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had commanded the archers not to leave their positions whatever happened.

When the archers saw the superiority of the Muslims and witnessed the signs of victory, their mouths watered for the spoils and booty, so they came down to them and left their positions. The disbelievers seized the opportunity and encircled the Muslims, and indeed the battle turned (ma'at), and although we were not defeated, we did not achieve victory, even though God the Exalted had promised His messengers victory and promised His army triumph. He, glory be to Him, said: "And Our word has already preceded to Our servants, the messengers, that they would surely be helped, and that Our soldiers would surely be the victorious" (al-Saffat 37:171–173).

So when you see a soldier of Islam being defeated, know that he has opposed the directive: either he opposed the Messenger's directive, or he opposed the directive of the commander appointed by the Messenger.

When the archers saw the superiority of the Muslims and witnessed the signs of victory, their mouths watered for the spoils and booty, so they came down to them and left their positions. The disbelievers seized the opportunity and encircled the Muslims, and indeed the battle turned (ma'at), and although we were not defeated, we did not achieve victory, even though God the Exalted had promised His messengers victory and promised His army triumph. He, glory be to Him, said: "And Our word has already preceded to Our servants, the messengers, that they would surely be helped, and that Our soldiers would surely be the victorious" (al-Saffat 37:171–173).

Nevertheless, the lack of victory at Uhud was a healthy sign in faith, because if the Muslims had won despite opposing the Messenger's command, his command would have become trivial to them afterwards, and they would have said: "We opposed him at Uhud and we won." So when you see a soldier of Islam being defeated, know that he has opposed the directive: either he opposed the Messenger's directive, or he opposed the directive of the commander appointed by the Messenger.

So: God's law of victory has not failed; rather, the soldiery for God failed. Therefore we say that at Uhud the Muslims were not victorious, but Islam was victorious and its commands were victorious.

Likewise, the Truthful, glory be to Him, warned us against arrogance and pride in strength and multitude of numbers, because victory in reality is not by the multitude of your numbers; rather, victory is from God. This lesson we learned at the battle of Hunayn. Abu Bakr himself felt something of that when he saw the numbers of the Muslims compared with the numbers of the disbelievers, and he said: "We will not be defeated today for lack of numbers." So God gave them a lesson never to be forgotten, and victory nearly went to the disbelievers, but the mercy of God overtook them, and God showed compassion to them at the end of the battle, and the matter was decided in favour of Islam.

So: pride and conceit contradict the rules of soldiery; victory is not by numbers nor by equipment, but victory is from God, as He, glory be to Him, said: "Fight them; God will punish them at your hands, and disgrace them, and help you against them, and heal the breasts of a believing people" (al-Tawbah 9:14).

And He said: "And you did not throw when you threw, but God threw" (al-Anfal 8:17).

So we say: since God has informed us of the dispute of the people of the Fire, it is a true reality, and we believe in its truthfulness.

Then the Truthful, glory be to Him, wished to give His Prophet (ﷺ) an argument, so He said:

"Say: I am only a warner..." (Sad 38:65).

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 38, verses 65–66:

We understand these verses in light of what the Qur'an recounts at the beginning of the surah concerning the disbelievers' denial of the Messenger. In the first verses of the surah, the Most High says: ﴿They wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves, and the disbelievers say, "This is a lying sorcerer. Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing."﴾ [Sad: 4–5], up to their saying: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?" Rather, they are in doubt about My Reminder. Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment.﴾ [Sad: 8].

So, the opening verses show that these people had a defect in two matters. The first is the matter of monotheism (tawhid): ﴿Has he made the gods into one God..?﴾ [Sad: 5]. The second is the matter of prophethood (nubuwwah): ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us..?﴾ [Sad: 8].

These verses came to answer them and to correct this defect. Here He says: (Say), O Muhammad: ﴿Indeed, I am only a warner..﴾ [Sad: 65]. He chose here the word *al-indhar* (warning) even though the Messenger (ﷺ) came as *bashir wa nadhir* (a bringer of good news and a warner), because the discourse here is in confrontation with the disbelievers, so warning fits them. As for the other matter, He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿There is no god except Allah, the One, the Subduer. Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, the Mighty, the Forgiving.﴾ [Sad: 65–66].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 38, verses 67-70:

The meaning of (naba') is the important news that has behind it realities which reality does not deny.

He said in Surat (al-Naba'): ﴿About what are they asking each other? About the great news﴾ [al-Naba': 1-2]. It was described as great because two matters will follow from it, relating to this world and the Hereafter. If you have taken your share in following your desires in this world, and this world has an end, then in the Hereafter you will burn in a fire that has no end.

You should have paid attention to this matter, because a person must define his purpose in existence. The true purpose is the one beyond which there is nothing further. As for a purpose beyond which there is a further one, it is not a purpose at all, but a stage that leads to what comes after it. Like the student who succeeds in the entrance examination, for example, and that success leads him to the preparatory school, and success in the preparatory school leads him to secondary school, and secondary school leads him to university.

And so on, even if he obtains a doctorate, he moves on to further stages, and then death. Even death is not the end of the journey; rather, after it, one goes either to a fire or to a garden. This is the purpose beyond which there is nothing further, because it is everlasting and eternal, with no end.

Therefore, the Truth, glorified is He, alerts us to this purpose. Say (O Muhammad): ﴿It is a great news. You turn away from it﴾ [Sad: 67-68].

The word (mu'rid), meaning "turning away," is what we describe when we say: "So-and-so gave me the breadth of his shoulders," meaning he turned away from me and left. This word is an image of the state of people when they are called to spend and when they are called to do good. Some of them turn away from it, and turning away happens in stages: first he turns his face away and twists his neck, then he gives you his side, then he exaggerates and turns his back to you.

The Qur'an has depicted this scene for us, and the Almighty said, describing the outcome of turning away from spending in the way of God: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of God, give them tidings of a painful punishment. On the Day they will be heated in the fire of Hell, and their foreheads and their sides and their backs will be branded with them..﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34-35].

Thus the recompense is of the same kind as the deed, and in the same order as the turning away in this world, there is branding in the Hereafter: ﴿This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard﴾ [al-Tawbah: 35].

So: the organs that took part in turning away are the ones that will be branded, and the branding is extended according to the extent of the turning away.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, wanted to demonstrate that Muhammad does not know the unseen, so He said: ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they were disputing﴾ [Sad: 69], because He had previously spoken of the dispute of the people of the Fire, saying: ﴿Indeed, that is true: the dispute of the people of the Fire﴾ [Sad: 64]. And He, glorified is He, clarified the dispute of the Exalted Assembly of angels at the beginning, when they said to the Truth, glorified is He: ﴿Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. This is their dispute, not that they dispute as humans dispute, because Allah said of them: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants. They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26-27].

The exchange that took place between Him, glorified is He, and the angels was named (takhasum, "dispute"), as if they were jealous for God lest He create another creation, the humans, who would disobey Him and cause corruption on earth, as the jinn had caused corruption before.

Then He, glorified is He, explains that Muhammad does not know the unseen, but that God informs him of it by revelation: ﴿It is only revealed to me that I am a clear warner﴾ [Sad: 70]. The One who informed me of what preceded informs me of what is to come, and this is an elevation in knowledge of the unseen.

The unseen has a veil that conceals it from us, a veil that conceals the past and a veil that conceals the future. The past is concealed by time, because ancient time, for example, had no recording of its events, and if there was a recording, it is a distorted recording, since it reflects human opinions, and human opinions must differ.

Likewise, the future conceals the time to come: you do not know what will happen in the future. As for the present we live in, its time is one but its place differs, so its veil is place. You now know what happens in your place, but you do not know what happens in other places.

The meaning is that the One who first informed me that the angels said such-and-such is the One who informed me of the dispute of the people of the Fire. Therefore, it is true.

He also said here: ﴿a clear warner﴾ [Sad: 70], meaning manifest, because the address is not to the believers who receive good tidings, but to the opponents, so it suits them: ﴿I am only a clear warner﴾ [Sad: 70].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 38, verses 71–74:

This statement came from the Truth, glorified and exalted be He, to the angels as a piece of information. But they understood it to be a consultation, and that the Creator, glorified be He, was consulting them about the matter of creating man. Therefore they said what they said. Yet they should have been alert to the fact that the matter had been decided and settled, since Allah had informed them of it by His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to create...﴾ [Sad: 71], in this emphatic form.

Here we must point out that some people try to take exception to the words of Allah concerning the creation of man from clay. They say: the Qur'an says once "from clay" (tin), and once "from water" (ma'), and once "from black mud altered" (hama' masnun), and once "from clay like pottery" (salsal). In reality, these are stages of one thing, not differing beginnings from which it was taken. Earth, when placed upon water, becomes clay (tin). When the clay is left until it becomes foul and its smell changes, it is hama' masnun. When it dries and hardens, it is salsal, like pottery.

When Allah created man, He created him from clay, meaning that he combines all the elements of the black, yellow and sandy soil, etc. Scholars have concluded that this soil is the one suitable for cultivation, because if the clay or soil is cohesive, it holds water beneath the root, so the plant rots and wilts; and if it is sandy, the water seeps away before the plant can absorb it.

So: one needs soil of a middle state, which holds water to the extent that allows the plant to benefit from it and absorb its nutrients, and then the remainder seeps away without harming the roots.

Scholars have also concluded that the elements of the human body amount to 16 elements, beginning with oxygen at 67%, which is the highest proportion, and ending with manganese. And that clay contains these same sixteen elements, and this proves the truthfulness of the Truth, glorified be He, regarding the creation of man from clay.

The meaning of ﴿So when I have proportioned him...﴾ [Sad: 72] is: I have shaped his form and figure. ﴿And breathed into him of My spirit...﴾ [Sad: 72] means he becomes a complete creature in whom life stirs and moves. ﴿Then fall down to him in prostration﴾ [Sad: 72] means: fall down prostrating. It was not prostration of worship; it was prostration of obedience to the one who commanded the prostration.

So: the angels' prostration was not to Adam himself; it was to Allah, who created Adam and commanded the angels to prostrate to him. The meaning of "prostrate to him" is like when you say: "I prostrate toward the qiblah," for prostration is not to the qiblah itself but toward its direction. ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely, except Iblis; he was arrogant and was among the disbelievers﴾ [Sad: 73–74].

They say: the Qur'an says once "from clay" (tin), and once "from water" (ma'), and once "from black mud altered" (hama' masnun), and once "from clay like pottery" (salsal). In reality, these are stages of one thing, not differing beginnings from which it was taken. Earth, when placed upon water, becomes clay (tin). When the clay is left until it becomes foul and its smell changes, it is hama' masnun. When it dries and hardens, it is salsal, like pottery.

When Allah created man, He created him from clay, meaning that he combines all the elements of the black, yellow and sandy soil, etc. Scholars have concluded that this soil is the one suitable for cultivation, because if the clay or soil is cohesive, it holds water beneath the root, so the plant rots and wilts; and if it is sandy, the water seeps away before the plant can absorb it.

So: one needs soil of a middle state, which holds water to the extent that allows the plant to benefit from it and absorb its nutrients, and then the remainder seeps away without harming the roots.

Scholars have also concluded that the elements of the human body amount to 16 elements, beginning with oxygen at 67%, which is the highest proportion, and ending with manganese. And that clay contains these same sixteen elements, and this proves the truthfulness of the Truth, glorified be He, regarding the creation of man from clay.

The meaning of ﴿So when I have proportioned him...﴾ [Sad: 72] is: I have shaped his form and figure. ﴿And breathed into him of My spirit...﴾ [Sad: 72] means he becomes a complete creature in whom life stirs and moves. ﴿Then fall down to him in prostration﴾ [Sad: 72] means: fall down prostrating. It was not prostration of worship; it was prostration of obedience to the one who commanded the prostration.

So: the angels' prostration was not to Adam himself; it was to Allah, who created Adam and commanded the angels to prostrate to him. The meaning of "prostrate to him" is like when you say: "I prostrate toward the qiblah," for prostration is not to the qiblah itself but toward its direction. ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely, except Iblis; he was arrogant and was among the disbelievers﴾ [Sad: 73–74].

The meaning of "prostrate to him" is like when you say: "I prostrate toward the qiblah," for prostration is not to the qiblah itself but toward its direction. ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely, except Iblis; he was arrogant and was among the disbelievers﴾ [Sad: 73–74].

Whoever follows this story finds that the Qur'an relates it in seven surahs, each in a different style. Sometimes it says: ﴿He refused...﴾ (Al-Hijr 15:31), and sometimes: ﴿He refused and was arrogant...﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:34).

The first matter we wish to clarify in this story is that Allah, the Exalted, did not make the Garden from which Adam descended to the earth the Garden of Refuge (jannat al-ma'wa), because he was not created for the Garden and then expelled from it through his disobedience. Rather, Adam was created for vicegerency (khilafa) on earth. In the first announcement made about him by Allah, the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, I am placing on the earth a vicegerent...﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:30).

So he was created for the earth. Since he is the father of all humankind, and humankind is of two kinds, one kind infallible (ma'sum), namely the messengers, and the other kind not infallible, namely ordinary people, it was necessary that what is established for both kinds should be embodied in Adam. Adam disobeyed first, then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and afterwards protected him from sin. Therefore Adam did not disobey while he was a prophet; he disobeyed before prophethood.

When the Exalted presented this matter, saying: ﴿Indeed, I am placing on the earth a vicegerent...﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:30), He, in His justice and mercy, did not wish to send Adam down to the earth to populate it without any method that would set right the movement of life. Nor did He wish to test him first with the obligation. So He made for him a piece of land containing all the components of life and its luxuries, and settled him in it, to train him in guidance and obligation through the commands "do" and "do not do."

He permitted him to eat from everything in this garden except one tree, from which He forbade him even to draw near, so that he would learn permission in what is lawful and prohibition in what is forbidden. Then He reminded him of Satan's enmity toward him, and warned him against Satan and his whispering.

But Satan misled Adam, so he ate from the tree he had been forbidden, and the violation he committed resulted in his nakedness appearing for the first time. Here there is a symbolic indication that nakedness does not appear in society except through the violation of Allah's method.

We also pause at the words: ﴿And do not approach this tree...﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:35). He, glorified be He, did not say "do not eat from this tree," but forbade merely approaching it, because whoever hovers around the protected zone (al-hima) is about to fall into it.

Therefore, when the Exalted speaks of the limits that He has made lawful for us, He says: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:229). But regarding the limits He has forbidden, He says: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:187).

In the verse before us we note His saying: ﴿O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating...﴾ (Sad 38:75), whereas in Al-A'raf He said: ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating...﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:12). One is affirmative and the other negative, yet the meaning is one, because the speaker of these words is Allah, Lord of the worlds. The meaning of ﴿What prevented you from prostrating...﴾ (Sad 38:75) is: you wanted to prostrate, but a hindrance intervened. As for ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating...﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:12), it means: did some preventer stop you, so that you did not prostrate against your will?

His saying: ﴿...for what I created with My hands...﴾ (Sad 38:75) explains the nobility of this creature. Its nobility is sufficient in that Allah attributed its creation directly to Himself. ﴿Have you become arrogant, or were you among the haughty (al-'alin)?﴾ (Sad 38:75) means: the reason that led you not to prostrate is either your arrogance in refusing to prostrate to Adam, or that you were among the haughty?

The scholars have differed about the meaning of al-'alin. Some said: they are the tyrants who are arrogant, who turn away from the rulings of Allah and His method out of arrogance. Among this usage is His saying concerning Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh was haughty in the land, and indeed he was among the transgressors﴾ (Yunus 10:83). He also said: ﴿That is the Last Abode; We grant it to those who do not desire exaltation in the earth or corruption, and the outcome is for the righteous﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:83). That is, exaltation over the rulings of Allah and over the commands of Allah.

Others said: al-'alin are a kind of angels, those who were not included in the command to prostrate to Adam. Those commanded to prostrate were the angels who had a connection with this creature, namely the ones who arrange affairs (al-mudabbirat), about whom Allah said: ﴿And those who arrange affairs (fa-l-mudabbirati amra)﴾ (Al-Nazi'at 79:5), and the successive angels (al-mu'aqqibat), about whom Allah said: ﴿For him are successive [angels] before him and behind him, who guard him by the command of Allah...﴾ (Al-Ra'd 13:11). These are the ones who were commanded to prostrate. As for al-'alun, they are angels whose only work is glorifying Allah, who have no connection with this universe and know nothing of it.

Thus the meaning of ﴿or were you among the haughty?﴾ (Sad 38:75) is: those who were not included in the command to prostrate. This meaning is closer to the truth, because Allah said before it: ﴿Have you become arrogant...?﴾ (Sad 38:75). So we should not interpret al-'alin after it as meaning "the arrogant," because that would give the same meaning as the first.

Here we should point out the scholars' disagreement about the nature of Iblis. Some said he is one of the angels; others said he is one of the jinn. Those of the first opinion rely on His saying: ﴿When your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to create a human from clay. So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down in prostration to him"﴾ (Sad 38:71-72). They said: then Iblis is one of the angels, because the command was addressed to them. The proof of this is that when he disobeyed and refused to prostrate, he was punished; so he was included in the command, and Allah did not command anyone except the angels. Had he not been an angel, he would not have been punished.

Our reply to the proponents of this view is that we must distinguish between proof by implication or inference (dalil al-iltizam aw al-istinbat), and textual proof (dalil al-nass). When there is a explicit text, there is no room for proof by implication or inference. Allah, the Exalted, has said in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿Except Iblis; he was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ (Al-Kahf 18:50). How, then, does the verse state explicitly that he is of the jinn, while we say he is of the angels?

As for why Allah held him accountable for not prostrating if he was of the jinn, we say: the angels are compelled to obedience; it is an innate disposition in them: ﴿They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ (Al-Tahrim 66:6). But humans and jinn are given choice between faith and disbelief, and between obedience and disobedience. So if one of them binds himself to obedience such that he does not disobey, he is more excellent than the angels, because the angels are compelled to obey, whereas he is obedient by his own choice while being capable of disobedience.

Therefore, that excellence was his, since he compelled himself to obey. Iblis was at this rank so much so that it was said he was the "peacock of the angels" because of his superiority over them. When the command was issued to the angels, it included him as well. For if he was of higher rank than the angels in the state of obedience, then he should have obeyed the command; and if he was lower than the angels, then a command addressed to the higher implies a command addressed to the lower.

To illustrate this matter, we say: if the President of the Republic enters and the ministers stand for him, then the standing of the deputy ministers is all the more fitting. In this way we settle this disagreement, away from fruitless argument.

His saying: ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely, except Iblis; he was arrogant and was among the disbelievers﴾ (Sad 38:73-74) is evidence that he was a created being endowed with choice, like a human who obeys and disobeys, as He said: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve...﴾ (Al-Kahf 18:29).

Then the Exalted relates Iblis's words in reply to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic:

﴿He said: "I am better than him..."﴾ (Sad 38:76).

Yes, Adam was created from clay, and Iblis was created from fire. But who said that clay is lower than fire, or that fire is higher than clay? A created thing does not gain rank and distinction by its substance; it gains its distinction from the One who created it. Therefore there is no substance higher than another, for God created them all and assigned each of them a task in life, so in their creation they are equal before God.

For this reason we have said: God gave the means (al-asbab) to the believer and to the disbeliever as a gift of lordship (ʿaṭāʾ rubūbiyya). But when the believer believed, God singled him out with another gift, the gift of divinity (ʿaṭāʾ al-ulūhiyya) in worship.

So when Iblis disobeyed God's command and claimed this superiority over Adam:

﴿He said, "Then get out of it...﴾

Al-Rajim: the one who is driven away from the mercy of God, deprived of every good. This meaning is then reinforced by ﴿And upon you is My curse until the Day of Judgment﴾ [Sad: 78], until the Day of Resurrection. Then Iblis responded, after God had cursed him and driven him away from His mercy:

﴿He said, "My Lord, then reprieve me until the day they are resurrected."﴾

Al-Rajim: the one who is driven away from the mercy of God, deprived of every good. This meaning is then reinforced by ﴿And upon you is My curse until the Day of Judgment﴾ [Sad: 78], until the Day of Resurrection. Then Iblis responded, after God had cursed him and driven him away from His mercy:

﴿He said, "My Lord, then reprieve me until the day they are resurrected."﴾

Al-Sha'rawi, Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66), on surah 38, verses 79–81:

Iblis says to the Lord of Glory: ﴿Then give me respite﴾ [Sad: 79], i.e., postpone my term. Thus he knows that every being has a specified term that it cannot exceed. Iblis's saying to his Lord, ﴿Then give me respite﴾ [Sad: 79], exposes his words to Adam when he wanted to seduce him into eating from the tree: ﴿Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120]. For if the tree of eternity were true, why would you ask your Lord to postpone your term? This also indicates Adam's heedlessness; had he paid attention to this matter, he would not have eaten from the tree.

We also understand from this that Iblis himself (the great teacher, al-Mu'allim al-Kabir) is the one who undertook the seduction of Adam, and did not leave this task to one of his offspring. Why? They said: because Adam had come to be in the rank of the angels, so a small devil from among the offspring is not fitting for him; rather, the great one, Iblis, is.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, answers Iblis in what he asked, saying to him: ﴿Indeed, you are among those given respite﴾ [Sad: 80], the postponed, ﴿until the Day of the time made known﴾ [Sad: 81], i.e., until the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 38, verse 82:

It indicates that Iblis knew how to swear an oath when he said: ﴿By Your might﴾, meaning: by Your might, O Lord, over Your creation, and Your independence from them, and from their obedience and their faith: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29].

So from this door I entered upon them, and from this door I will mislead them all. I do not take them from You, O Lord, and whoever You want of them, I cannot approach him, as is shown by His saying after it: ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾. Thus: Your might over them is what made me greedy for them.

Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 38, verse 83:

This verse indicates that the enmity is not between Iblis and his Lord, but between Iblis and the children of Adam. It also indicates that Iblis knew how to swear an oath when he said: ﴿So by Your might...﴾ [Sad: 82], meaning: by Your might, O Lord, concerning Your creation, and Your independence from them, and from their obedience and their faith, ﴿so whoever wills may believe, and whoever wills may disbelieve...﴾ [al-Kahf: 29].

From this door I entered upon them, and from this door I will mislead them all, for I do not take them from You, O Lord; and whomever You desire among them, I cannot approach him. The evidence is His saying after it: ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [Sad: 83]. Thus: Your might concerning them is what made me covet them.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 38, verses 84–85:

The speech here belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿He said: "Then the truth—and the truth I say—﴾ [Sad: 84], meaning: what We do to you is the truth. ﴿And the truth I say﴾ [Sad: 84], meaning: I say nothing but the truth, and nothing is required of me but the truth, because I am the Truth (al-Haqq). Then, glory be to Him, He explains the intended truth which Allah has spoken and decreed: ﴿"I will surely fill Hell with you and with those among them who follow you, all together."﴾ [Sad: 85], meaning: with you, and with your offspring, and with those among them who follow you, that is, from the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), namely the nation of the call (ummat al-da'wa), which includes both those who believed and those who disbelieved.

They say: Is this a prior judgment from Allah, Exalted, upon the creatures who will come after? If the matter were so, then it would be compulsion and coercion. The reality is that Allah, Exalted, decreed this for them by His knowledge of what would proceed from them by their own choice, not by compelling them to act. Because of His knowledge of what would be, He decreed it, and there is in the matter neither compulsion nor coercion.

We have given an example for this issue—and to Allah belongs the highest example—saying: The teacher in the classroom, through his knowledge of the level of the students, can determine their results, so he says: So-and-so will pass and so-and-so will fail. By his knowledge of their academic level he has judged them, and he has no part in the examination or in its grading.

(Say) an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): ﴿Say: I do not ask you any wage for it⁠—﴾ [Sad: 86]. Had he said, "I do not ask you any wage (ajran) for it," the meaning would also have been sound. But his saying ﴿min ajr⟩ [Sad: 86] here, with min (from), indicates the smallest thing that can be called a wage, even a single pound or a single piastre. Thus it negates any wage at all. The word ajr, on the other hand, means a substantial wage that is counted of value, and it does not preclude a small wage. Just as you say: "I have no money," and "I have no money at all," meaning: not even from the very beginning of what is called money, not even a single piastre.

That Allah, glorified is He, says to His Prophet (ﷺ): "Say to them, O Muhammad: I do not ask them for any wage for it," is as if He were saying to them: "O people, what Muhammad has brought you is a beneficial work for you, in your religion and in your worldly life, and it was incumbent upon you to give him a wage for it." Therefore, he deserves a wage, but he will not ask you for it, because what he offers you cannot be repaid or compensated by any human being. Its reward is received only from Allah; He alone is able to recompense him and to give him in return for what he has presented.

Therefore, Muhammad (ﷺ) deserves a wage for guiding the people and conveying to them the method of their Lord. He is not indifferent to this wage; rather, he wants this work to be valued by the One who sent him with this message.

This statement, ﴿Say: I do not ask you any wage for it⁠—﴾ [Sad: 86], is a necessary sunnah (practice) common to all the Prophets, for all of them said it to their peoples, except Sayyidna Ibrahim and Sayyidna Musa, peace be upon them. Why?

They said: because Sayyidna Ibrahim, when he first called to faith in Allah and His oneness, called his father Azar, and it was not fitting for him to ask a wage from his father. Likewise, Sayyidna Musa, when he first called to faith, called Pharaoh, who had raised him and done good to him, so how could he say to him, "Give me my wage"?

As for His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And I am not of those who pretend⁠—﴾ [Sad: 86]. The mutakallif (pretender) is one who affects something and displays a thing beyond his due measure. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not burden yourselves beyond your capacity." That is: do not impose upon yourselves beyond your ability, like the one who borrows in order to fulfil the duty of hospitality, then the guest leaves and the debt remains upon him; this makes him resent the guest afterwards and be pained when he visits him.

Therefore: be upon your natural disposition, and perform the duty of hospitality according to your capacity. And why not, when your exemplar (ﷺ) says: ﴿And I am not of those who pretend⁠—﴾ [Sad: 86]? Because the matter he brought does not require any artificial effort at persuasion, since it is a matter in accord with human nature.

You may review the rulings of the Sharia and consider them: are they sound in themselves or not? The religion tells you: do not lie. So who says that good lies in lying? The religion tells you: do not cheat. So who says that righteousness lies in cheating? The religion has forbidden you from drinking wine, so who says it is beneficial? And who denies that it corrupts the intellect, by which alone man was honoured?

Therefore: all these are clear rulings that need no artificial effort at persuasion, because they accord with the sound innate nature (fitrah).

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds⁠—﴾ [Sad: 87]. That is: the Qur'an is nothing but a reminder to the worlds. Remembrance and reminding arise only from forgetting a prior thing which we want to remind you of. So the Qur'an is a reminder in the sense that it reminds you of what you have forgotten from the first covenant, the covenant of fitrah, which Allah took from you while you were in the stage of the atoms (dhar), when He said: ﴿Am I not your Lord?⁠﻿﻿ [al-A'raf: 172], and all acknowledged it: ﴿They said: Yes⁠—﻿ [al-A'raf: 172].

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: so keep this covenant and remember this acknowledgment, ﴿lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: Indeed we were unaware of this. Or you should say: Only our fathers associated partners with Allah before, and we were offspring after them⁠—﴾ [al-A'raf: 172-173].

Therefore: Allah, exalted is He, does not impose upon you this acknowledgment; rather He reminds you of it, because the obligation was taken from you on the day you were an atom in the loins of your father Adam, when you had no desire.

So His saying about the Qur'an, ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds⁠—﴾ [Sad: 87], indicates that what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought, from the summit of the tawhid of Allah and faith in Him down to the subsidiary details and particulars of the obligations, is a matter that existed of old, which all recognised and acknowledged, and the Qur'an only reminds of this first covenant.

Then the surah concludes with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will surely know its news after a while⁠—﴾ [Sad: 88]. That is: those who denied the Qur'an will come to know the consequence of this denial, and they will know that it is a true report; they will know that ﴿after a while⁠—﴾ [Sad: 88]. Some said: "the while" refers to the manifestation of Islam and its victory over disbelief, beginning from the battle of Badr, until a speaker said: "I am amazed at this unlettered man, how he conquered half the world in half a century." Indeed, this is a marvel that still persists until now.

These deniers saw with their own eyes the victory of Islam and the defeat of disbelief, and they saw the territory of the land of disbelief diminishing and the territory of the land of faith increasing, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts?⁠—﴾ [al-Ra'd: 41]. Yet they did not take warning from the conquests of Islam.

Others said: "the while" refers to the Resurrection, when these deniers enter the Fire; then they will know the truth of this speech which Allah informed them of in His Qur'an.

The word naba' (news) is said only of a great and important report, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Say: It is a mighty news⁠—﴾ [Sad: 67], ﴿from which you turn away⁠—﴾ [Sad: 68].

So what about a news which He described as great, He being Allah? The greatness of news is in proportion to the good it brings to a person. The news that you have succeeded in admission is other than the news of your success in the secondary-school certificate, which is other than the news that you have become a minister. So the greatness of news is according to the good hoped for from it for the human being.

Therefore: what of the good that awaits you after performing the divine obligations? It is a good that makes you happy not only in your passing worldly life, but makes you happy in your enduring, everlasting hereafter. The greatness of this news is that it guarantees for you both lives, the worldly and the hereafter.

And I ask Allah, at the end of the surah, to make us of the portion of His saying: ﴿And you will surely know its news after a while⁠—﴾ [Sad: 88].

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds.﴾ That is: it (i.e., the Qur'an) is nothing but a reminder to the worlds. Remembrance and reminding arise only from forgetting something that came before, and We want to remind you of it. So the Qur'an is a reminder in the sense that it reminds you of what you forgot from the first covenant, the covenant of the innate nature (fitrah) which God took from you while you were in the stage of the atoms (tawr al-dharr). He said: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], and all of them acknowledged it: ﴿They said: Yes indeed!﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]. Then God Almighty said: So hold fast to this covenant and remember this acknowledgment, lest you say on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Indeed, we were unaware of this﴾ — ﴿or lest you say: Only our forefathers associated partners with God before, and we were offspring after them﴾ [al-A'raf: 172–173].

So: the Truth, glorified is He, does not impose this acknowledgment upon you; rather He reminds you of it, because the obligation was taken from you on the day you were a speck in the loins of your father Adam, when you had no desire.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 38, verse 88:

His (Allah's) saying, Exalted is He, concerning the Qur'an: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾, indicates that what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought, from the summit of the tawhid (oneness) of Allah and belief in Him down to the secondary matters of legal obligation (taklif) and its particulars, is a matter that existed in the past, which everyone knew and acknowledged. The Qur'an merely reminds (mudhakkir) of this primordial covenant.

Then the surah concludes with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you will surely come to know its news after a while﴾. That is: those who denied the Qur'an will come to know the consequence of this denial, and they will know that it is a true report. They will know this "after a while." Some said: "The while (al-hin) is intended to mean the manifestation of Islam and its victory over disbelief, beginning from the battle of Badr, until a speaker said: 'I am amazed at this Unlettered one (al-ummi), how he conquered half the world in half a century.' Yes, this is a marvel, and it continues to be so until now."

These deniers had witnessed with their own eyes the victory of Islam and the defeat of disbelief, and they saw the territory of the land of disbelief shrinking and the territory of the land of faith expanding, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outskirts?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 41]. Yet despite this, they did not take heed from the conquests of Islam.

Others said: "The while is intended to mean the Resurrection, when these deniers enter the Fire; then they will know the truth of this statement which Allah informed them of in His Book."

The word naba' (news) is only used for a great and important report, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Say: It is a mighty news, from which you turn away﴾ [Sad: 67–68].

So what about a naba' whose description Allah Himself gave as "mighty"? The greatness of news comes in proportion to the good it brings to a person. The news that you have been accepted is different from the news of your success in the secondary school certificate (tawjihiyya) exam, which is different from the news that you have become a minister. The greatness of news is in proportion to the good it carries for a person, which is hoped for from it.

Therefore: what about the good that awaits you after you fulfil the divine obligations? It is a good that does not make you happy in your passing worldly life only, but makes you happy in your enduring, eternal hereafter. So the greatness of this news is that it guarantees for you both lives, the worldly and the hereafter.

And I ask Allah at the end of the surah to make us have a share of His saying: ﴿And you will surely come to know its news after a while﴾.
